title_en: Hotel giant Wyndham exposed customer data after app security lapse
title_fa: Hotel giant Wyndham exposed customer data after app security lapse
excerpt_en: Exclusive: Wyndham left a hardcoded credential in its customer app, allowing anyone to access customer data. The hotel giant wouldn't say if it has the ability to check for any past unauthorized access.
excerpt_fa: Exclusive: Wyndham left a hardcoded credential in its customer app, allowing anyone to access customer data. The hotel giant wouldn't say if it has the ability to check for any past unauthorized access.
content_en:
Hotel and resort giant Wyndham has acknowledged a cybersecurity incident after a good-faith security researcher discovered a bug that allowed anyone to access customers’ personal information.
Security researcher Robert Wiggins at What Security exclusively told TechCrunch that he found a password inside the source code of Wyndham’s Android app, which granted access to an internal company database, hosted by tech company Salesforce.
Wiggins told TechCrunch that the credential exposed personal information including customer names, email addresses, and Wyndham member numbers. The database also stores customer login tokens (called JWTs) that keep customers logged-in to their apps without having to repeatedly enter their own passwords. The database also contained Wyndham files and documents.
According to Wiggins, the database had millions of entries, but he was unable to determine an accurate number of exposed customer records. Wyndham touts some 129 million enrolled rewards members.
The researcher said Wyndham has no way to report security flaws, and asked for TechCrunch’s help in alerting the company. Soon after TechCrunch made contact with Wyndham’s cybersecurity staff, the exposed credential was revoked, preventing any further access to the database.
“Our team has taken steps to address the issue,” a Wyndham spokesperson told TechCrunch. “Our security teams have no evidence of any unauthorized access,” the statement added, without providing any further details about the claim.
Wyndham’s spokesperson would not say, when asked, whether the company had the technical means, such as server logs, to determine if anyone had access to the customer database prior to Wiggins’ discovery.
TechCrunch also asked Wyndham whether it planned to notify customers whose information was exposed, or disclose the incident to U.S. regulators, such as filing a notice with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, as public companies are required to do for material cybersecurity incidents. Wyndham would not say.
Wyndham’s spokesperson also would not say for how long the password was embedded in its customer app, or how Wyndham plans to ship a long-term fix for the app.
App and software developers generally avoid including passwords or credentials in publicly released software and apps — a process known as “hardcoding” — as anyone with a copy of the software can extract the password and use it to access its associated server or database. Given the simplicity with which credentials can be abused by anyone, many cases of hardcoded credentials are automatically scored with a maximum vulnerability severity rating.
For Wiggins, this is his second public discovery of hardcoded credentials in two weeks, after finding a near-identical vulnerability in Applebee’s app that exposed customer data. Wiggins relied on AI tools for both discoveries, which make it easier to identify simple security weaknesses, such as hardcoded credentials, by scouring thousands of lines of decompiled app code every second.
When asked about Wyndham’s response, Wiggins told TechCrunch that he was glad the company fixed the issue, but noted that without visibility into any past activity, someone with malicious intent could have leaked large amounts of customers’ personal information.
The company would not say whether it planned to set up a vulnerability disclosure program to allow outside security researchers and hackers to privately report security vulnerabilities.
Michael Francess, Wyndham’s cybersecurity director who responded to the incident, told TechCrunch that researchers can alert [email protected] with details of potential security issues. The company’s spokesperson would not say whether it plans to change its website to allow researchers to alert the company.
This is the latest known security incident at Wyndham in recent years. In 2024, a security researcher found several Wyndham hotel check-in desks were running remote-access spyware that was leaking screenshots of guest records and booking information to the open web.
Soon after our reporting, the spyware app found on the hotel computers, called pcTattletale, was hacked and its banks of customer data stolen, forcing the company’s owner, Bryan Fleming, to shut down the company. Fleming, a former resident of Michigan, was later arrested by federal authorities and convicted of making, selling, and advertising unlawful spyware.

title_en: The pros and cons of using mesh Wi-Fi
title_fa: The pros and cons of using mesh Wi-Fi
excerpt_en: Should you buy a mesh Wi-Fi system or a standalone router? Learn how each handles range, roaming, and cost, and which one fits your home best.
excerpt_fa: Should you buy a mesh Wi-Fi system or a standalone router? Learn how each handles range, roaming, and cost, and which one fits your home best.
content_en:
The pros and cons of using mesh Wi-Fi
Mesh covers more ground, but a standalone router may be all you need.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
Diving into Wi-Fi routers for the first time can be baffling. There are a lot of concepts to understand, and not just the differences between Wi-Fi 6 and 7. Speeds and features vary between models using the same specification, and it may not be clear which of your devices can (or should) connect to which frequency bands.
One of the biggest purchasing decisions is whether to go with a mesh Wi-Fi system or stick to a standalone router. Most people probably default to standalone products, since they're cheaper. In fact, given the price gap, it's important to have concrete reasons for stepping up to a mesh product.
The value of mesh systems mostly boils down to range and seamless roaming. In some situations, however, a standalone router may not only be acceptable, but preferable. Here's how to decide which option is right for you.
The benefits and drawbacks of mesh Wi-Fi
The main advantage of mesh Wi-Fi is range. In a mesh system, each satellite router acts as a sort of repeater for the gateway router that connects to your modem or fiber terminal. In theory, a relatively cheap kit like an Eero 7 two-pack can cover up to 4,000 square feet. If you need more coverage, you just add another compatible router. Conversely, standalone products have a fixed coverage radius unless you buy a Wi-Fi extender.
Unlike extenders, mesh systems enable seamless transitions. There are no separate SSIDs (network IDs) — they simply hand devices off from one unit to another based on how close they are. This avoids the hassle of manual SSID selection and the problems that sometimes arise when devices need to talk to each other and assume a shared network. You also get more consistent speeds, as a signal should never degrade much unless you roam into the wider world.
This seamlessness comes with downsides beyond price. Since mesh products depend on unified SSIDs, you can't assign separate IDs for each frequency band; band steering is automatic. I know from experience that mesh routers can trip up cheap 2.4GHz-only smart home accessories because their setup apps often can't find them when your phone is on 5 or 6GHz. On the flip side, you might want to force devices like PCs or VR headsets over to 5 or 6GHz for the best possible bandwidth.
It's also worth noting that with cheaper mesh products, the backhaul between routers sometimes shares the same bands as connecting devices. When that happens, performance can suffer considerably. If you don't have the budget for a tri- or quad-band system, there may not be much point in going with mesh technology unless filling in dead zones is all that matters.
When should you choose mesh Wi-Fi?
Mesh is the obvious choice if you live in a multi-floor house, or want coverage in your backyard, detached shed or garage. A standalone router can cause smart home conflicts and create slow or dead zones, especially since metal and concrete can block signals. When interference persists, some mesh systems will even let you set up a wired Ethernet backhaul as a workaround.
Most apartments should be thoroughly covered by a standalone router unless you're encountering specific speed or range issues. You're better off saving your money or putting the savings toward a faster router.
There are some borderline cases. For instance, some multi-floor homes are small enough to be covered by a single router. If you want to push the limits, place your router in a relatively central location, and keep it unobscured by anything that might harm signal quality. Think of your router as a radio station — you wouldn't expect to hear the news clearly if the broadcast tower were on the opposite side of a mountain.

title_en: A short seller flagged Nvidia CEO’s ties to a suspected Chinese spy six months before the scandal
title_fa: A short seller flagged Nvidia CEO’s ties to a suspected Chinese spy six months before the scandal
excerpt_en: Six months before Nvidia's spy scandal erupted, Culper Research was already questioning Jensen Huang's unusually close relationship with a Chinese executive.
excerpt_fa: Six months before Nvidia's spy scandal erupted, Culper Research was already questioning Jensen Huang's unusually close relationship with a Chinese executive.
content_en:
Six months before the Nvidia spy scandal emerged, the New York-based short seller firm Culper Research had already raised questions about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s unusually close relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that buys Nvidia chips. She is now suspected to be a Chinese spy.
The Nvidia CEO admitted to an extramarital affair over the weekend, and the company has now opened a formal investigation into his relationship with Alice Huang (who shares his last name but is not related). U.S. intelligence officials believe she was recruited by the Chinese government to collect intelligence on Jensen Huang and influence his position regarding U.S. export controls on advanced AI chips.
Culper’s May 13 report is resurfacing because it picked up on the connection between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang while investigating Megaspeed’s ties to Nvidia.
In particular, the report called the relationship between the two executives “uncomfortably close,” noting that the Nvidia CEO was spotted partying and socializing with Alice Huang on multiple occasions. The report even claimed that some Nvidia employees wondered whether they had a “special relationship.”
Culper Research also theorized the China business that Nvidia lost to export controls had been rerouted through Southeast Asia, and that Megaspeed, a major chip buyer in the region, was secretly financed by Chinese tech giant Alibaba through shell companies. It pointed to financial records that showed Megaspeed’s total liabilities and equity had grown from $33 million at the end of 2023 to around $3 billion by the end of 2024, much of it in the form of refundable deposits from an unidentified source.
Financial Times reported Monday that documents show Alibaba lent money to Megaspeed through subsidiaries.
Culper is a short seller, so it stood to financially benefit from making these allegations, and those about possible illegal chip diversion have not been independently verified. Its report is available on the web and was posted to X back in May.

title_en: The race is on to sue Nvidia
title_fa: The race is on to sue Nvidia
excerpt_en: Nvidia’s stock slid more than 4% after its board opened an investigation into Jensen Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, and one securities law expert says the company’s earlier insistence that it was all “normal” could turn into a very expensive problem.
excerpt_fa: Nvidia’s stock slid more than 4% after its board opened an investigation into Jensen Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, and one securities law expert says the company’s earlier insistence that it was all “normal” could turn into a very expensive problem.
content_en:
Nvidia’s stock slid more than 4% on Monday, the first trading day after its board said it would investigate CEO Jensen Huang over his relationship with Alice Huang, an executive U.S. intelligence believes was spying for China.
Securities lawyers were already moving. At least four firms, including Schall, Brown & Schwartz and Levi & Korsinsky, announced investigations Monday into whether Nvidia misled investors. Robert Bartlett, a Stanford Law professor and securities law expert, expects them to have plenty of company.
“I would definitely wager that there’ll be a filing,” Bartlett said in an interview Monday morning, adding that he wouldn’t be surprised if a case had been filed by the end of the day. Plaintiffs’ lawyers have good reasons to be first in line; under federal securities law, the first complaint triggers a public notice, and investors then have 60 days to ask the court to be named lead plaintiff. A firm that files early gets a head start on signing up investors with large losses, as well as on shaping the story of the case. Bartlett was right, in fact. A case surfaced Monday afternoon in the Northern District of California, where Nvidia is headquartered.
Rosen Law Firm, a New York-based plaintiffs’ firm that specializes in securities class actions, filed it on behalf of Mark Kistenmacher, a retail investor who made seven purchases totaling roughly $20,500 this year, according to a schedule attached to the complaint. (Rosen was lead counsel in a $250 million settlement with Alibaba and ranks among the most active filers of such cases.) The proposed class covers anyone who bought Nvidia securities between Oct. 9, 2025, and Nov. 8, 2026, and the suit names both Nvidia and Huang.
The complaint accuses them of misleading investors about Huang’s ties to Megaspeed, the Singapore-based data center outfit where Alice Huang was considered a top exec, and it points to three statements as proof: Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo’s late-October claim that Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang were “not unusual or unexpected,” the company’s even earlier claim that it found “no evidence of diversion” of its chips, and Jensen Huang’s Oct. 30 comment to Bloomberg that Nvidia’s dealings with Megaspeed were “normal and not unusual.”
All three were false or misleading, the suit says, because Huang was having an affair with Alice Huang. Kistenmacher is asking for unspecified damages, interest and attorneys’ fees, and he wants a jury trial.
While much remains unknown, the legal theory here doesn’t depend on anything the board’s investigation may turn up about Huang’s private life. When The New York Times first reported on Huang’s ties to Alice Huang last month, Rizzo really did tell the Times that the relationship was “not unusual or unexpected.” Rizzo separately told another outlet, The Hill, that “Megaspeed has been no different than many other regional cloud customers. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.”
Of course, the world now knows that was not true. Worse, the Times reports that U.S. intelligence had been monitoring Alice Huang for more than a year.
From a securities perspective, Bartlett said, the company’s earlier statement was “clearly a misleading statement.” And because Huang is CEO, Bartlett said, “his knowledge gets imputed to the company.” In other words, Nvidia is treated as having known what its chief executive knew.
The Kistenmacher complaint makes the same argument.
Bartlett predicted a “classic fraud on the market” claim, in which investors argue they paid prices that reflected false or incomplete public information, and lost money when the truth emerged. This early lawsuit relies on that theory, and Monday’s drop of $7.97 per share, or 4.27%, gives the attorneys involved a lot to work with. Damages in such cases are tied to the stock’s decline, and Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies in the world, so you can imagine a settlement could prove exceedingly expensive.
That means a large payment from the company and its directors-and-officers insurers, but typically no personal consequences for the CEO or the board. It is also a civil matter, so Huang isn’t facing prison over it. The irony, as Bartlett noted, is that the suit is brought in the name of Nvidia’s shareholders, and shareholders ultimately pay for the settlement, directly or through insurance premiums.
Bartlett sorted Nvidia’s wider exposure into buckets. The first is the securities fraud claim, which is the clearest immediate problem for the company and potentially for Huang. The second is governance: what the board knew and when. It’s possible directors were kept in the dark, but the board also has oversight duties, and once the Times began reporting on the Megaspeed connection, the company should have had reporting lines to bring a critical risk like this to directors. If it didn’t, or if directors didn’t act, board-level liability is possible.
A third category, one that would change everything, would arise only if the board’s investigation finds Huang knew about the intelligence connection. That would be “a whole other ball game,” as Bartlett said. (The board said in a statement to the public Sunday that it has no reason to believe national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.)
There’s also the question of government action. The SEC can seek an officer-and-director bar for intentional securities-fraud violations, which Bartlett said is technically on the table. But he doubts the current SEC under Chairman Paul Atkins would have the appetite, given President Trump’s support for Huang. A roughly two-year clock after discovery of the facts would leave room for a future administration to act, but the window would be tight, and Bartlett posited that’s pretty unlikely when asked about it.
It’s worth underscoring that neither law firm announcements nor this newly filed complaint is a sign of a strong case. Plaintiffs’ firms are quick...

One of the best upgrades you can make to your PC gaming setup is an OLED monitor. Fortunately, MSI’s factory-reconditioned Mag 272QP X24 is on sale at Woot through November 18th with a 180-day manufacturer warranty for $290.99, which is more than $100 cheaper than the full MSRP of $399.99.
MSI’s refurbished QD-OLED gaming monitor is on sale for under $300
The 1440p, 240Hz panel offers a potentially sizable upgrade from older IPS panels.
The 1440p, 240Hz panel offers a potentially sizable upgrade from older IPS panels.
MSI’s 27-inch screen is well-featured for the price, with 1440p resolution, a 240Hz refresh rate, and both G-Sync and FreeSync compatibility, which help reduce screen tearing when your FPS is below the max refresh rate. PC games are particularly well-suited to take advantage of the deep black levels OLED panels produce, too, giving every game you play a deeper, more immersive feel. MSI’s budget OLED also features quantum dots for fuller, more vivid colors. It doesn’t cut corners on ports either, with two HDMI 2.1, one DisplayPort 1.4a, and one USB Type-C DP Alt input.

content_en:
At this point, reading through the latest splashy pledge to use AI for the good of the environment feels like downing a nonalcoholic beer. Admittedly, I’m suspicious from the onset. How can this be good? But I love beer and our planet enough to give it a whirl — and hey, why not try a little harm reduction?
The global pledge to use AI for climate good is a cruel joke
A pledge to make AI less of an environmental disaster is floating around United Nations climate negotiations this month, but it’s just lip service.
A pledge to make AI less of an environmental disaster is floating around United Nations climate negotiations this month, but it’s just lip service.
Negotiators from more than 190 countries around the world are in Antalya, Turkey, this month for the annual United Nations climate summit, called COP31 (the 31st “Conference of the Parties” that ratified the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change). Turkey previewed its Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge ahead of the convening, inviting delegates from other countries to endorse the pledge before its official launch on November 16th.
Like that nonalcoholic beer, it’s deeply unsatisfying
The pledge actually includes some common sense measures that could curb planet-heating pollution from energy-hungry AI data centers. Unfortunately, like that nonalcoholic beer, it’s deeply unsatisfying.
At first glance, many of the ingredients you’d expect from a real commitment on AI’s environmental impact are here. It sets out to ensure that data centers are increasingly powered by clean energy, calling for internationally recognized standards for responsible AI development. Similarly, it pushes for reporting requirements so that there’s greater transparency into the impact data centers — which run primarily on fossil fuels — already have on the environment. It even acknowledges the need to manage the tons of e-waste created by the generative AI boom.
And yet, there is no there there because, as the text states clearly, “these objectives of the pledge are voluntary and non-prescriptive, create no new obligations, and are to be implemented in accordance with national circumstances.” In other words, these are voluntary commitments that countries can choose to follow or not follow based on their whims.
There’s also no way this pledge will garner the support of the most influential player in this game (at least for now). The US has way more data centers than any other country, but Donald Trump has pulled the nation out of the global climate accord and has no official delegates at the summit in Turkey.
The last point in the pledge is to ensure that advances in generative AI can be used to create more renewable energy and reduce greenhouse gas emissions, particularly in economically developing countries. To that end, research published in a Nature journal in August found that AI causes more carbon emissions by boosting fossil fuel production than it would help avoid through gains in renewable energy.
When it comes down to it, this pledge offers a placebo effect at best. In the face of data centers demanding tremendous amounts of electricity and spurring the development of more fossil fuel infrastructure, negotiators can’t be seen as doing nothing about the issue. And with global average temperatures still on the rise, we could all use an emotional support beverage.

title_en: YouTube will once again be part of Billboard chart calculations in 2027
title_fa: YouTube will once again be part of Billboard chart calculations in 2027
excerpt_en: Billboard will give more weight to free, ad-supported listening in its methodology.
excerpt_fa: Billboard will give more weight to free, ad-supported listening in its methodology.
content_en:
YouTube will once again be part of Billboard chart calculations in 2027
Billboard will give more weight to free, ad-supported listening in its methodology.
Starting next year, YouTube performance will once again factor into where music places on the Billboard charts. The Google-owned platform opted to stop sharing its data with Billboard in December 2025, claiming that the charts didn't assign sufficient value to free, ad-supported listening in their calculations.
Performance on streaming platforms is included in the results of the Billboard 200 and Hot 100 charts, as well as in its album genre charts and multi-metric song charts, but Billboard has long weighted listens from paid subscribers over free ones. That policy still holds, but Billboard announced today that it will adjust the math regarding the margin between free and paid listens. Beginning in January 2027, the company will count 1,500 ad-supported streams as an album consumption unit, which is the equivalent of selling one album or getting 1,000 streams from paying listeners. Under Billboard's previous calculations, 2,500 ad-supported streams were required to make one album consumption unit.
As a result of these new equivalence rules, YouTube is now willing to share its data with the charting company again. The update to its previous announcement about withdrawing from Billboard's accounts simply states: "We are returning to the Billboard charts starting in 2027. Billboard's new methodology better reflects how fans engage with music today across both subscription and ad-supported services."

title_en: 5 Nintendo Switch 2 features everyone should know about
title_fa: 5 Nintendo Switch 2 features everyone should know about
excerpt_en: From finding hidden controllers to sharing games with others, improve your gaming experience on the Nintendo Switch 2 with these useful features.
excerpt_fa: From finding hidden controllers to sharing games with others, improve your gaming experience on the Nintendo Switch 2 with these useful features.
content_en:
5 Nintendo Switch 2 features everyone should know about
The Switch 2 has lots of little tricks to discover: some inherited from the original Switch and some new.
Chances are that you aren't taking full advantage of everything your Nintendo Switch 2 can do. It's easy to jump right into games and ignore the various settings that help your system run at its best.
The Switch 2 is a pretty direct upgrade to the original Switch — its design, OS, controllers and other aspects are refinements rather than something entirely new. That means many of the Switch 1's tips and tricks work on the newer console too, so if you're a Switch veteran you might already know where to look. But there are other easy-to-miss improvements to find, and they're unique to the newer system.
Whether it's making controls more comfortable or repurposing hardware you already have, you should know about the Switch 2's neat little features. For instance, you might have overlooked the option to share games with friends, which can save you all money. Try these features out before you jump into a game on your next session.
Locate your controllers
The Joy-Con 2 controllers are larger than the original models but still small enough to sink between the couch cushions or lose sight of underneath a blanket. Next time you can't find your controllers, your console can help. Open the Controllers page from the main menu, then hit Search for Controllers.
All compatible controllers you've paired to the system will appear; to find one, highlight it and hold L or R (or press the touchscreen). While you're holding the button, the controller will vibrate and play a sound, helping you track it down. If you can't find one, try walking around with the console to get back in range of it.
There are a few caveats here. While you can pair original Switch controllers with a Switch 2, this feature can't locate them. Third-party Switch controllers may or may not work. You can't ping a dead controller with this, and it won't find a controller that's paired with another console.
Preserve long-term battery health
Most laptops, phones and similar devices now include a feature to cap their charging at 80 percent (or similar values). This is designed to protect the health of the device's battery over several years, since keeping lithium-ion batteries at 100 percent for extended periods wears them faster than lower percentages.
Your Switch 2 can also do this: open Settings and scroll to System. About halfway down, you'll see a toggle titled Stop Charging Around 80-90%. Turn this on, and your system will limit itself when it's on the dock or otherwise charging. If you're headed on a long trip, feel free to shut this off first to fully juice up. But in general, especially if your Switch 2 sits on the dock most of the time, this is worth having on.
Speaking of charging, the System Battery (%) option next to this is appreciated, too. It will show the exact battery level instead of a general symbol.
Remap your controller buttons
While many modern games have expansive control scheme options, sometimes you can't adjust exactly what you'd like. For those cases, you're able to remap buttons at the system level. Open Settings and go to Accessibility. At the top, choose Button Mapping — if you plan to use this often, enable Button Mapping in Quick Settings and a shortcut to this tool will appear when you hold the Home button.
In this menu, you'll see each connected controller on the left side. Select one and choose Edit Controller's Mappings to show its buttons, where you're free to remap most of the inputs to anything else. For example, you could swap the ZR and ZL buttons with R and L, or move an inconvenient input to a button that's in closer reach.
The C button is of particular interest; if you don't use GameChat, you can disable the button to avoid accidental activation. Alternatively, turn it into a secondary input for another button, like a D-pad direction or pressing one of the sticks. Check the Control Stick Settings if you'd like to swap the left and right sticks or use a Joy-Con 2 vertically when a game intends you to hold it horizontally.
While you can't apply a remap to a certain game, you can save up to five profiles per controller and swap them as needed. After hitting Save, choose Save as a Preset and give it a name. When remapping is applied, you'll see a blue wrench icon at the bottom-left of the menu and anywhere else that controller icon appears. Games are not aware of remapping done this way, so if you've swapped ZR and R, for example, you'll need to press the latter when the game prompts the former.
There's one more related option at the bottom of Settings > Controllers & Accessories: Swap A and B. This simple toggle does what it says and is great if you're used to PlayStation or Xbox controllers that have the Confirm button at the bottom and Cancel on the right.
Share games with family and friends
You have options for letting others enjoy your games, thanks to Nintendo's virtual game cards. Any game loaded onto your system is playable by all other users on the console under their own profile. If you have a Nintendo family group set up, other members can borrow your games on their system for two weeks (during which time you're unable to play them).
Open the Virtual Game Cards page on the Home screen to see your collection. Choose one and hit Lend to Family Group Member, then Select a User to Lend To. 5 Nintendo Switch 2 features everyone should know about
The Switch 2 has lots of little tricks to discover: some inherited from the original Switch and some new.
Chances are that you aren't taking full advantage of everything your Nintendo Switch 2 can do. It's easy to jump right into games and ignore the various settings that help your system run at its best.
The Switch 2 is a pretty direct upgrade to the original Switch — its design, OS, controllers and other aspects are refinements rather than something entirely new. That means many of the Switch 1's tips and tricks work on the newer console too, so if you're a Switch veteran you might already know where to look. But there are other easy-to-miss improvements to find, and they're unique to the newer system.
Whether it's making controls more comfortable or repurposing hardware you already have, you should know about the Switch 2's neat little features. For instance, you might have overlooked the option to share games with friends, which can save you all money. Try these features out before you jump into a game on your next session.
Locate your controllers
The Joy-Con 2 controllers are larger than the original models but still small enough to sink between the couch cushions or lose sight of underneath a blanket. Next time you can't find your controllers, your console can help. Open the Controllers page from the main menu, then hit Search for Controllers.
All compatible controllers you've paired to the system will appear; to find one, highlight it and hold L or R (or press the touchscreen). While you're holding the button, the controller will vibrate and play a sound, helping you track it down. If you can't find one, try walking around with the console to get back in range of it.

Most laptops, phones and similar devices now include a feature to cap their charging at 80 percent (or similar values). This is designed to protect the health of the device's battery over several years, since keeping lithium-ion batteries at 100 percent for extended periods wears them faster than lower percentages.
Your Switch 2 can also do this: open Settings and scroll to System. About halfway down, you'll see a toggle titled Stop Charging Around 80-90%. Turn this on, and your system will limit itself when it's on the dock or otherwise charging. If you're headed on a long trip, feel free to shut this off first to fully juice up. But in general, especially if your Switch 2 sits on the dock most of the time, this is worth having on.
Speaking of charging, the System Battery (%) option next to this is appreciated, too. It will show the exact battery level instead of a general symbol.

While many modern games have expansive control scheme options, sometimes you can't adjust exactly what you'd like. For those cases, you're able to remap buttons at the system level. Select one and choose Edit Controller's Mappings to show its buttons, where you're free to remap most of the inputs to anything else. title_en: Apple starts offering $50 extended usage packs for AI features in Creator Studio
title_fa: Apple starts offering $50 extended usage packs for AI features in Creator Studio
excerpt_en: It'll cost you to access Logic Pro's AI assistant after you reach the monthly usage limit.
excerpt_fa: It'll cost you to access Logic Pro's AI assistant after you reach the monthly usage limit.
content_en:
Apple starts offering $50 extended usage packs for AI features in Creator Studio
It’ll cost you to access Logic Pro’s AI assistant after you reach the monthly usage limit.
Apple has made it clear for a while that Siri AI is bound by daily usage limits and that it will offer expanded access via iCloud+ plans. The company hasn't shed more light on exactly how that will work, but it has revealed how Creator Studio users can continue wielding the AI features of those apps after they reach the regular limits.
It has started selling $50 intelligence usage packs for Creator Studio, and Logic Pro is the first app to support these. Apple updated Logic Pro last month to include an assistant that's powered by its own models as well as those from third parties. The company said the chatbot can help "creators and producers navigate production workflows, start a new song, set up a vocal track from a single prompt or refine an active project."
As noted by 9to5Mac, folks can view their AI usage in the app by going to Logic Pro on the menu bar, then Intelligence Features > Show Usage. The window that pops up includes a Buy More Usage button — clicking this takes you to the option to buy an intelligence usage pack.
A support page explains that users with active Apple Creator Studio subscriptions in the US, UK, Canada, Brazil, France, Germany, India and Mexico can buy intelligence usage packs to keep using AI features after they reach their monthly usage limit. A pack is tied to the Apple Account used to purchase it — there's no Family Sharing support.
"Unused additional usage purchased with intelligence usage packs roll over from month to month and expire 12 months after purchase," Apple added. "Additional usage gets consumed for relevant features only after you've reached your monthly limit in any given month."
It seems likely that Apple will expand intelligence usage packs to other Creator Studio apps, such as Final Cut Pro and Pixelmator Pro. It's interesting that Apple is opting for this approach over a regular subscription, but perhaps the company has other offerings planned for the future. For what it's worth, Creator Studio apps are available via a subscription or one-time purchase.

title_en: Fervo now has $12B in orders for its geothermal power tech
title_fa: Fervo now has $12B in orders for its geothermal power tech
excerpt_en: Geothermal company Fervo is targeting natural gas as it brings down geothermal drilling costs at its 8.4 GW resource in Utah.
excerpt_fa: Geothermal company Fervo is targeting natural gas as it brings down geothermal drilling costs at its 8.4 GW resource in Utah.
content_en:
Geothermal company Fervo couldn’t have picked a better time to deliver its first power plants.
In its third-quarter earnings report, released Monday, the company said it now has $11.9 billion worth of contracted revenue on the books, up from $7.2 billion last quarter.
Fervo has been hitting its deadlines recently, which undoubtedly has helped to drive orders.
As hyperscalers scour the earth for electricity to power their AI data centers, Fervo is on track to complete a 396 megawatt power plant for Google by the end of 2028. The geothermal company connected its first 100 megawatt power plant to the grid earlier this year.
Both projects are built at Cape Station in Utah, a resource that could generate 8.4 gigawatts of electricity. Previously, experts told Fervo the site could only produce about 4 gigawatts.
The Google project, now called Cape Google 400, will be grid connected, co-founder and CEO Tim Latimer said in an earnings call Monday. The arrangement means that Google can draw power from the deal and sell it to other customers if it’s not ready to use it.
“We built Cape Station on our schedule. Google can develop a potential data center on their schedule, and neither party is waiting on the other,” he said.
Latimer’s statement also underlines an advantage that geothermal has over competing generating sources like large nuclear or natural gas power plants — the phased nature of its construction.
Fervo’s newer wells are deeper and hotter, each capable of generating 15 megawatts gross power, and several are linked together into what the company calls a GeoBlock. The first completed GeoBlock generated 33 megawatts, while recent ones hit 50 megawatts. They’re sized to match the demand of a typical data center hall, so hyperscalers can bring them online as they’re completed.
As a business, Fervo is still in the early stages. It ended the quarter with an operating loss of $43.7 million, though it holds cash and cash equivalents of $1.9 billion and long-term debt of $301.6 million, which should give it plenty of runway.
Much will depend on the company bringing down the cost of its power plants. While hyperscalers are hungry for power today, they may not always be as price-indiscriminate.
Yet if Fervo can deliver on its promises, it could end up winning on price. The first phase of its Cape Station project cost $7,000 per kilowatt of capacity, the company said. The cost for its Google project is $5,500 per kilowatt, a significant drop that suggests Fervo is on the right path. With subsidies, that’s about equivalent to a new natural gas power plant running on fuel that costs $6 per million BTUs. Still about twice what natural gas costs today, but trending closer to where it needs to be.
But if Fervo can hit its long-term target of $3,000 per kilowatt, it could significantly undercut natural gas power, even at today’s prices. That’s a pretty ambitious target, but the company has made significant strides in just a few years. No wonder Google is getting in early.

title_en: Jensen Huang pulls out of ElevenLabs Summit amid Nvidia controversy
title_fa: Jensen Huang pulls out of ElevenLabs Summit amid Nvidia controversy
excerpt_en: The Nvidia CEO also pulled out of an Anthropic event earlier.
excerpt_fa: The Nvidia CEO also pulled out of an Anthropic event earlier.
content_en:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has pulled out of the ElevenLabs Summit scheduled for this Wednesday in New York, ElevenLabs, the voice AI company, confirmed Monday. He has also dropped out of other speaking engagements, including the Anthropic CEO Forum. Nvidia is an investor in ElevenLabs.
The withdrawals come after Huang admitted to an extramarital affair over the weekend, and Nvidia opened an investigation into his relationship with a possible Chinese spy.
“I owe my family and all of you an apology. I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” Huang said in a memo to the company.
The incident has rattled the AI industry, raising questions about Huang’s staying power as CEO and Nvidia’s own China ambitions.

title_en: Windows 11 is finally adding an easier way to disable the Sticky Keys pop-up
title_fa: Windows 11 is finally adding an easier way to disable the Sticky Keys pop-up
excerpt_en: There's a checkbox that simply turns it off.
excerpt_fa: There's a checkbox that simply turns it off.
content_en:
Windows 11 is finally adding an easier way to disable the Sticky Keys pop-up
There’s a checkbox that simply turns it off.
Microsoft is finally making it easier to disable the Sticky Keys pop-up. This window shows up whenever a user hits Shift five times in succession and lets users activate multi-key shortcuts, like Ctrl+Alt+Del, with a single key.
There's just one problem. Sticky Keys are incredibly useful as an accessibility feature, but not everyone needs them. However, the pop-up rears its head each and every time Shift is pressed five times consecutively. This has been a frustration for long-time Windows users who have no interest in Sticky Keys and are annoyed by constant pop-ups. Shift is the default button for many actions in PC games, including sprinting and walking.
We're adding the ability to permanently turn off the prompt to enable sticky keys from the pop up itself pic.twitter.com/kWBYmGPA6M
— Jen Gentleman 🌺 (@JenMsft) November 7, 2026
The solution is downright simple. The pop-up now arrives with a checkbox that says "never turn on Sticky Keys with this shortcut." Clicking the checkbox ensures the annoying window goes away permanently.
There's a spot of bad news here. The checkbox is currently only available to those enrolled in the Windows Insider program. It's just an experimental beta release for now. However, this has been a long-requested feature so it's likely to make the jump to all Windows 11 users in the future.
There's a more traditional way to turn off Sticky Keys, while we wait for general availability. Navigate to "Settings" and then "Accessibility" and finally "Keyboard." Make sure "Sticky Keys" is toggled to the off position. Next, make sure "Keyboard shortcut for Sticky Keys" is also toggled to the off position.
It might be hard to believe, but those wacky Sticky Keys are more than 30 years old. They were first introduced in Windows 95.

title_en: YouTube streaming data returns to Billboard charts, ending major disagreement
title_fa: YouTube streaming data returns to Billboard charts, ending major disagreement
excerpt_en: YouTube will resume sharing streaming data with Billboard in 2027 after changes to the chart formula give more weight to free, ad-supported music streams.
excerpt_fa: YouTube will resume sharing streaming data with Billboard in 2027 after changes to the chart formula give more weight to free, ad-supported music streams.
content_en:
YouTube is officially returning to the Billboard charts, ending a disagreement over how music streams should count toward chart rankings.
Announced Monday, YouTube is set to resume sharing its streaming data with Billboard in 2027. The decision follows recent changes to Billboard’s chart formula, which now gives more weight to ad-supported streams.
The disagreement began in December 2025, when YouTube said it would stop sharing its streaming data with Billboard. The company argued that the chart formula favored paid subscriptions while not giving enough credit to fans who listen for free with ads.
At the time, Lyor Cohen, YouTube’s global head of music, criticized the system in a blog post, saying it didn’t reflect how people listen to music today.
“Billboard uses an outdated formula that weights subscription-supported streams higher than ad-supported. This doesn’t reflect how fans engage with music today and ignores the massive engagement from fans who don’t have a subscription. Streaming is the primary way people experience music, making up 84% of U.S. recorded music revenue,” Cohen wrote.
Under Billboard’s previous formula, 1,000 paid streams counted the same as 2,500 ad-supported streams. YouTube felt this gave too much importance to paid listening, especially when millions of fans discover and support artists through free streaming.
Billboard has now updated its formula, reducing the gap between the two types of streams. Under the new system, 1,000 paid streams will equal 1,500 ad-supported streams when calculating album consumption units, compared with 2,500 under the previous formula. Paid streams will still count for more, but free streams will now have a bigger impact on chart positions.
YouTube’s return could make a difference for many artists, especially independent musicians and those with large international fan bases. Music videos, live performances, lyric videos, and other content on the platform help artists reach new audiences. With YouTube’s data back in the mix, more of that activity will now count toward their Billboard performance.
For Billboard, getting YouTube’s data back also means having a more complete picture of how people listen to and discover music. With so many fans using the platform, leaving its streams out meant missing a major part of music consumption.

title_en: How to use your iPhone to take the best picture of the Moon
title_fa: How to use your iPhone to take the best picture of the Moon
excerpt_en: We explain how to take the best photos of the Moon with your iPhone, regardless of which model.
excerpt_fa: We explain how to take the best photos of the Moon with your iPhone, regardless of which model.
content_en:
How to use your iPhone to take the best picture of the Moon
With some easy adjustments, you can upgrade your lunar shots.
Trying to snap a picture of the moon with your iPhone can be an exercise in frustration. You frame it up and everything seems fine, but after clicking the shutter, your photo is either a ball of light with no detail or a blurred mess.
So what happened, and what can you do about it? Even with fancy AI algorithms, cameras can't break the laws of physics when shooting a bright object at night. And unlike some devices, iPhone cameras don't resort to trickery when taking lunar snaps, so the photo quality is entirely up to you and how you set the camera. Here's how to do it right.
Why your moon shot is a featureless blob
Everyone wants their moon photos to be sharp and well exposed, showing all the craters and features you see with your naked eye. The challenge is that the Moon is very bright (it's illuminated by the Sun, after all) and the night sky is extremely dark. Your camera's exposure system always tries to average light, so it often overexposes to "brighten" the surrounding sky. As a result, the moon can often become overexposed and look like a textureless circle.
Your moon photos may also be blurry. This happens because when your iPhone tries to boost exposure, it must lower the shutter speed to 1/30th of a second or even lower. As a result, any hand shaking or other movement can blur the image, even with your iPhone's stabilization system.
Finally, you may find that the moon isn't large enough in your shots. The latest iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro models have up to an 8x "optical-quality" zoom and 40x digital zoom, while the iPhone 15 Pro and iPhone 16 Pro models offer a 5x optical zoom and 25x digital zoom. The iPhone 17 and iPhone 18 standard models have 4x optical and 10x digital zoom. Whatever model you own, zoom in as much as you can so that the moon is clearly visible.
Use a tripod
You can get a reasonable moon shot handheld, but your best bet is a tripod. Any cheap one will do, including models like the Amazon Basics 64-inch tripod that includes a smartphone holder. However, I'd recommend spending at least $20 on something higher quality and more adjustable, like the Amazon Basics 50-inch tripod. If you get one like that, you'll also need an inexpensive, tripod-compatible smartphone holder like this one.
If you're having trouble justifying the cost of a tripod, you can also use it for long exposures (to blur waterfalls or create traffic light trails), panoramas, hands-free TikTok-style recordings and video calls. If you really don't want to spend the money, though, you can prop your iPhone against a book or coffee cup, then use the iPhone camera's three-second timer (one of the six-dot menu options) to take the photo. Otherwise, you could jostle your phone when you hit the shutter button and your moon shot will be blurry.
Nail the zoom and exposure levels
While the recently-launched iPhone 18 Pro's native camera offers manual controls for shutter speed and ISO, older iPhones do not. However, you can adjust two separate exposure settings. The first of those is called exposure and the other is brightness.
To set the first, go to the six-dot menu and tap "Exposure," one of the nine settings on recent iPhones like my 16 Pro Max. Then drag the slider to the right to set it to -2EV, which lets in the least light. This setting will stay through your photo session as long as you don't close the Camera app.
Once your iPhone is set up, tap and hold on the moon for several seconds to lock the autofocus and exposure. Then, slide the "brightness" slider (with a sun icon) that appears to the right down to the desired setting (usually close to the minimum).
Once you do so, you'll start to see the moon's craters and detail appear. Make sure you can see the maximum detail possible, even if the brightness seems too low (you can always increase it after you take the photo). Then press the shutter button, and voila, you have a beautiful, clear shot of the moon. Note that both the exposure and brightness must be adjusted at or near the minimum possible, or your moon photo will lack detail.
If you want to capture video instead of a photo, follow the same process. Change your iPhone's setting to "Video," then zoom in on the moon (15x max for recent Pro cameras) and frame the shot. Make sure Exposure is at -2EV, then tap and hold on the moon to lock focus. Drag the brightness slider down to the desired setting until you see the level of detail you want. Then, hit the record button and capture the desired length of video. To extract a photo, play your video back, stop on the desired frame and take a screenshot.
Final thoughts
One quick note on resolution. You may notice that your iPhone moon pictures look pixelated. At 25x digital zoom, the effective resolution on an iPhone 15 Pro or 16 Pro (both with 12MP 5x telephoto cameras) is just 0.48 megapixels. The camera automatically upscales it to 12MP to match your other photos, but the detail is already lost. The iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro models do a bit better with their 48MP sensors and 4x optical zoom, which reduces to an effective 1.24MP resolution at a 25x zoom before upscaling.
If you want more control for moon photos than Apple's Camera app offers, you could upgrade to the iPhone 18 Pro, but the App Store also has other options. Moontake is a free app built for moon photography that uses the longest telephoto lens by default and sets the proper exposure automatically. It also displays astronomical data like the lunar azimuth and altitude. You can also use apps that give you granular control over all types of photography (ISO and shutter speed control), like Halide Mark III and ProCamera.
content_fa:
How to use your iPhone to take the best picture of the Moon
With some easy adjustments, you can upgrade your lunar shots.
Trying to snap a picture of the moon with your iPhone can be an exercise in frustration. You frame it up and everything seems fine, but after clicking the shutter, your photo is either a ball of light with no detail or a blurred mess.
So what happened, and what can you do about it? Even with fancy AI algorithms, cameras can't break the laws of physics when shooting a bright object at night. And unlike some devices, iPhone cameras don't resort to trickery when taking lunar snaps, so the photo quality is entirely up to you and how you set the camera. Here's how to do it right.
Why your moon shot is a featureless blob
Everyone wants their moon photos to be sharp and well exposed, showing all the craters and features you see with your naked eye. The challenge is that the Moon is very bright (it's illuminated by the Sun, after all) and the night sky is extremely dark. Your camera's exposure system always tries to average light, so it often overexposes to "brighten" the surrounding sky. As a result, the moon can often become overexposed and look like a textureless circle.
Your moon photos may also be blurry. This happens because when your iPhone tries to boost exposure, it must lower the shutter speed to 1/30th of a second or even lower. As a result, any hand shaking or other movement can blur the image, even with your iPhone's stabilization system.
Finally, you may find that the moon isn't large enough in your shots. The latest iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro models have up to an 8x "optical-quality" zoom and 40x digital zoom, while the iPhone 15 Pro and iPhone 16 Pro models offer a 5x optical zoom and 25x digital zoom. The iPhone 17 and iPhone 18 standard models have 4x optical and 10x digital zoom. Whatever model you own, zoom in as much as you can so that the moon is clearly visible.
Use a tripod
You can get a reasonable moon shot handheld, but your best bet is a tripod. Any cheap one will do, including models like the Amazon Basics 64-inch tripod that includes a smartphone holder. However, I'd recommend spending at least $20 on something higher quality and more adjustable, like the Amazon Basics 50-inch tripod. If you get one like that, you'll also need an inexpensive, tripod-compatible smartphone holder like this one.
If you're having trouble justifying the cost of a tripod, you can also use it for long exposures (to blur waterfalls or create traffic light trails), panoramas, hands-free TikTok-style recordings and video calls. If you really don't want to spend the money, though, you can prop your iPhone against a book or coffee cup, then use the iPhone camera's three-second timer (one of the six-dot menu options) to take the photo. Otherwise, you could jostle your phone when you hit the shutter button and your moon shot will be blurry.
Nail the zoom and exposure levels
While the recently-launched iPhone 18 Pro's native camera offers manual controls for shutter speed and ISO, older iPhones do not. However, you can adjust two separate exposure settings. The first of those is called exposure and the other is brightness.
To set the first, go to the six-dot menu and tap "Exposure," one of the nine settings on recent iPhones like my 16 Pro Max. Then drag the slider to the right to set it to -2EV, which lets in the least light. This setting will stay through your photo session as long as you don't close the Camera app.
Once your iPhone is set up, tap and hold on the moon for several seconds to lock the autofocus and exposure. Then, slide the "brightness" slider (with a sun icon) that appears to the right down to the desired setting (usually close to the minimum).
Once you do so, you'll start to see the moon's craters and detail appear. Make sure you can see the maximum detail possible, even if the brightness seems too low (you can always increase it after you take the photo). Then press the shutter button, and voila, you have a beautiful, clear shot of the moon. Note that both the exposure and brightness must be adjusted at or near the minimum possible, or your moon photo will lack detail.
If you want to capture video instead of a photo, follow the same process. Change your iPhone's setting to "Video," then zoom in on the moon (15x max for recent Pro cameras) and frame the shot. Make sure Exposure is at -2EV, then tap and hold on the moon to lock focus. Drag the brightness slider down to the desired setting until you see the level of detail you want. Then, hit the record button and capture the desired length of video. To extract a photo, play your video back, stop on the desired frame and take a screenshot.
Final thoughts
One quick note on resolution. You may notice that your iPhone moon pictures look pixelated. At 25x digital zoom, the effective resolution on an iPhone 15 Pro or 16 Pro (both with 12MP 5x telephoto cameras) is just 0.48 megapixels. The camera automatically upscales it to 12MP to match your other photos, but the detail is already lost. The iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro models do a bit better with their 48MP sensors and 4x optical zoom, which reduces to an effective 1.24MP resolution at a 25x zoom before upscaling.
If you want more control for moon photos than Apple's Camera app offers, you could upgrade to the iPhone 18 Pro, but the App Store also has other options. Moontake is a free app built for moon photography that uses the longest telephoto lens by default and sets the proper exposure automatically. It also displays astronomical data like the lunar azimuth and altitude. You can also use apps that give you granular control over all types of photography (ISO and shutter speed control), like Halide Mark III and ProCamera.

title_en: Anthropic releases new Mythos and Fable models amid RSI concerns
title_fa: Anthropic releases new Mythos and Fable models amid RSI concerns
excerpt_en: Anthropic says the new models "show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision," as well as in communicating more clearly with users.
excerpt_fa: Anthropic says the new models "show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision," as well as in communicating more clearly with users.
content_en:
Anthropic released new versions of its most advanced models on Monday, with the launch of Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2. The company says the new models “show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision” and communicate more clearly with users.
Notably, Anthropic is lowering the cost of Fable from $10 to $8 per million input tokens. As a result, Fable 5.2 is now cheaper than its primary competitor GPT-6 Astra. Anthropic says that the new version of Fable will return responses 30% faster across effort levels. Faster inference serving is available for double the price.
Fable 5.2 is also compatible with zero data retention (ZDR) policies through the Enterprise Frontier Safeguards system, long a sticking point for many enterprise clients.
It’s Anthropic’s first model release since the arrival of a third-party report from the assessment group METR, which suggested the lab might be approaching recursive self-improvement (RSI) — or the ability for AI models to carry on model training independently. The METR report found internal models were speeding up Anthropic’s AI progress by roughly 2x, although many uncertainties remain.
Still, Anthropic’s release notes significant ongoing challenges in accurately testing model capabilities. “Claude Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 each voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any of our recent models, which challenges our ability to assess how they will act in real-world settings. As these settings expand and capabilities increase with future models, we expect this challenge to grow.”
Anthropic maintains that the new version of Mythos does not have the ability to act covertly against its user, a verdict that’s detailed further in Mythos 5.2’s system card.
“Claude Mythos 5.2 shows stronger covert capabilities than prior Claude models on several of our evaluations, particularly when its reasoning is hidden from the monitor,” the system card reads. “That said, we believe that low levels of absolute performance on our new covert evaluations support claims that rely on detection of harmful actions in high-stakes situations.”
Fable 5.2 has been available to select parties in pre-release for some time, and Anthropic says the model has already “solved two open problems in theoretical physics, formalized Fermat’s Last Theorem, and supported numerous other research projects.”
Also on Monday, AI startup Physical Superintelligence announced a new proof of the Aaronson‑Ambainis conjecture, a pivotal step in setting theoretical limits for quantum computing. Notably, the lab said the result was achieved by running “a non-public Anthropic model” within PSI’s own system. Anthropic did not confirm or deny whether Fable 5.2 was the model in question.

title_en: AI hardware startup Nominal triples valuation to $3B in 8 months
title_fa: AI hardware startup Nominal triples valuation to $3B in 8 months
excerpt_en: Nominal, a startup that offers an AI platform for hardware engineering and claims Anduril as a major customer, has raised another big round of financing that triples its valuation.
excerpt_fa: Nominal, a startup that offers an AI platform for hardware engineering and claims Anduril as a major customer, has raised another big round of financing that triples its valuation.
content_en:
Nominal, a four-year-old, Austin-based startup that offers an AI platform purpose-built for engineering and testing complex hardware, like aircraft, nuclear reactors, and smart factories, has raised another big round of financing that triples its valuation. On Monday, it announced a $240 million Series C at a $3 billion valuation led by Lightspeed Venture Partners and co-led by Insight Partners.
This follows the company’s announcement in March of a $155 million Series B extension at a $1 billion valuation, led by Trae Stephens at Founders Fund. That round was a “preemptive” deal — meaning an offer initiated by the investor, not the startup. Other investors in the company include Sequoia, General Catalyst, and Lux Capital.
Nominal says that it has 80 commercial and government organizations as customers. One of its key customers is Anduril, the defense company co-founded by Stephens. Nominal also won a government contract in October when the Air Force selected it for a $71.2 million Strategic Funding Increase (STRATFI) investment, which is a program that requires matching funds from outside the Air Force.
Nominal CEO and co-founder Cameron McCord (pictured) is a former U.S. Navy submarine officer and an Anduril alum.

title_en: France blames Iran for mass-hacks targeting freezers in grocery stores and blood banks
title_fa: France blames Iran for mass-hacks targeting freezers in grocery stores and blood banks
excerpt_en: France's foreign minister blamed Iran for launching at least two waves of cyberattacks targeting industrial refrigerated and freezer units across France and wider Europe.
excerpt_fa: France's foreign minister blamed Iran for launching at least two waves of cyberattacks targeting industrial refrigerated and freezer units across France and wider Europe.
content_en:
The French government has formally blamed Iran for launching cyberattacks that targeted thousands of internet-connected industrial refrigerated and freezer units across the country and broader Europe.
This is the latest in a string of destructive cyberattacks attributed to Iran this year, following a spate of hacks targeting U.S. water providers and other online intrusions that caused mass-disruption to U.S. medical device maker Stryker and others.
The U.S. government linked the attacks to pro-Iranian hacktivists who are working for Tehran, likely in response to the U.S./Israel-led war against Iran which killed its supreme leader in February.
Two recent waves of cyberattacks throughout October and into November saw hackers remotely break into web-based controllers that manage fleets of industrial cold and chilling units at grocery stores and retail supermarkets, and raise the temperatures to spoil food and destroy goods. Medical blood banks were also hacked but the attacks were stopped before any blood was spoiled, according to the French Blood Establishment.
Security researchers have since warned that the web-based controllers are vulnerable to remote hacks, with some of the affected models made by Danish company Danfoss no longer receiving security fixes.
In a statement given to reporters in Paris on Monday, French foreign minister Jean-Noël Barrot said: “I am able to confirm that responsibility for this act lies with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps,” referring to Iran’s military and hackers.
“This was an attack of unprecedented scale and aggression; it represents the first large-scale act of sabotage on our national territory and constitutes a major assault on the nation’s interests and the security of the French people,” said Barrot, adding that the hacks will “not go without consequences.”
The French government has summoned Iran’s ambassador. Reuters first reported France’s attribution to Iran, citing sources ahead of the foreign minister’s remarks. The French government said it would also issue European-wide sanctions against those who carried out the hacks. Barrot said that the matter was now in the hands of the French justice system.
A spokesperson for Iran’s consulate in New York did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The U.S. government is also reportedly looking into whether freezer units on military bases were hacked, following reports of similar outages and disruption earlier this year. U.S. officials have reportedly also linked the freezer-related cyberattack to Iran, but the intelligence community has not yet made a formal or public attribution.

excerpt_en: After publishing a support article in early September outlining usage limits for some Apple Intelligence features, the company has updated Logic Pro with an option to "Buy More Usage" for a one-time purchase price of $49.99, as spotted by 9to5Mac. It has a built-in AI assistant...
excerpt_fa: After publishing a support article in early September outlining usage limits for some Apple Intelligence features, the company has updated Logic Pro with an option to "Buy More Usage" for a one-time purchase price of $49.99, as spotted by 9to5Mac. It has a built-in AI assistant...
content_en:
After publishing a support article in early September outlining usage limits for some Apple Intelligence features, the company has updated Logic Pro with an option to “Buy More Usage” for a one-time purchase price of $49.99, as spotted by 9to5Mac. It has a built-in AI assistant to do things like “start a new song, set up a vocal track from a single prompt, or refine an active project.”
Apple’s $50 Intelligence Usage Packs extend access to some AI features
Logic Pro is Apple’s first app to charge for extended usage of Apple Intelligence.
Logic Pro is Apple’s first app to charge for extended usage of Apple Intelligence.
These Intelligence Usage Packs, as Apple calls them, will allow users to continue accessing certain Apple Intelligence features that have usage limits because they rely on cloud-based AI models from OpenAI or Google Gemini. The Usage Packs can only be used by the Apple Account that purchased them (Family Sharing isn’t supported) and, as Apple explains on its website, any unused additional usage will roll over from month to month, but will expire 12 months after it was purchased.
For Logic Pro, Apple says the usage limit is “impacted by the complexity of conversations you have with the assistant.” Users finding themselves running out of access can find the option to buy an Intelligence Usage Pack in the Intelligence Features > Show Usage section of the app’s main menu. Currently, only Logic Pro has the option to buy more usage, but it’s expected to be added to other Apple Creator Studio apps this month, including Pixelmator Pro, Final Cut Pro, Motion, plus Pages, Keynote, and Numbers that are getting access to Apple’s AI chatbot.

Anthropic is announcing two new models today: Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, which it says are designed to take on “daunting” technical challenges. The company claims the new models show improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision, and can generate outputs faster than the 5.1 versions of the Fable and Mythos models.
Anthropic launches new Claude Fable and Mythos 5.2 models
Claude Fable 5.2 is designed to take on big technical challenges, and it’s available today.
Claude Fable 5.2 is designed to take on big technical challenges, and it’s available today.
Claude Fable 5.2 is good at challenging software engineering problems, Anthropic says, and can orchestrate agent teams and tackle long-running projects. The new model has also solved some complex scientific problems, including two open theoretical physics problems.
During prerelease testing, the two models have “helped our engineers complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours,” Anthropic says.
Claude Fable 5.2 is launching today. As for Claude Mythos 5.2, only vetted organizations will have access to start. The new 5.2 models follow the release of Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1 in September.

title_en: Gmail users should know about this little-noticed feature
title_fa: Gmail users should know about this little-noticed feature
excerpt_en: Gmail's unsend feature will delay it from dispatching your message. Here's how to extend the amount of time you have to use it.
excerpt_fa: Gmail's unsend feature will delay it from dispatching your message. Here's how to extend the amount of time you have to use it.
content_en:
Gmail users should know about this little-noticed feature
You can unsend messages on Gmail, but you only have seconds to act.
Whenever you hit Send on Gmail, a small box pops up in the bottom left corner of your screen that will let you undo the action before it's too late. It says Message sent along with the options Undo and View message. If you've suddenly spotted a typo or remembered a piece of information that you forgot to include in your original message, the "unsend" feature could be your best of friend. However, it only shows up for a very short of amount of time, and you have to hit Undo very, very quickly.
To be clear, the feature doesn't literally "unsend" an email that has already been sent. Once it's out there, you can't claw it back from your recipient's inbox, even if it hasn't been opened yet. What it does is delay the service from dispatching your email to give you the chance to stop it from going through. That is why you're only given a short amount of time to decide. Since it only delays your email from being sent, your intended recipient doesn't get notified about it and will not know that you've unsent an email. Take note that hitting View message before the waiting time ends also means you're ending your chance early to unsend your email.
How to extend Gmail's unsend message feature.
The good news is that you can lengthen the amount of time you have to hit Undo, so you can give your messages a quick final read before Gmail pushes them through. You'll have to manage your expectations, though: Even if you choose the longest amount of time available, it's still pretty short. And no, you still can't take back emails that have already landed in your recipient's inbox.
To choose and extend the amount of time you have to unsend a message, go to Gmail on desktop and click or tap on the Gear icon at the top right corner of the screen. In the Quick settings panel, choose See all settings. In the General settings page, scroll down until you see the Undo Send section, where you'll find the option to change your cancellation period.
It will be set to the feature's default of five seconds, but you can change it to 10, 20 or 30 seconds. That half-a-minute period is the longest you can delay your email's dispatch, but it could be long enough to prevent disaster when sending out especially important messages. Don't forget to hit Save changes at the bottom of the General settings page for the new cancellation period to take effect.

content_en:
The price of Xbox Game Pass Ultimate has fluctuated between $20 and $30 per month over the last year, but you can get three months of the top plan for around $19 per month. At Newegg, using the coupon code BNWF2656 at checkout knocks $11 off the usual cost of a three-month subscription. That brings the price down to just $57.99 for three months. In addition to full access to over 500 games on both Xbox consoles and Windows PC machines, the upgraded Ultimate plan includes EA Play and Ubisoft Plus Classics, which have their own libraries and benefits, and Fortnite Crew for full access to the Fortnite battles passes. On Xbox, Ultimate enables online multiplayer, as well.

title_en: How does Google Wallet's notification feed work and can you disable it?
title_fa: How does Google Wallet's notification feed work and can you disable it?
excerpt_en: Google Wallet is attempting to make notifications easier to find with a notification feed, but if you're sick of alerts, find out how to disable them.
excerpt_fa: Google Wallet is attempting to make notifications easier to find with a notification feed, but if you're sick of alerts, find out how to disable them.
content_en:
How does Google Wallet's notification feed work and can you disable it?
Here's how to check if you've received one of Google Wallet's latest feature rollouts.
If you've looked over the pros and cons of digital wallets and settled on Google's Wallet app, you'll be happy to know an update has dropped for the platform. This update, which began to roll out in October 2026, launched both increased passport recognition and an in-application notification inbox. This update has been added in an effort to have Google Wallet outdo Apple Wallet.
If you've received this new update, the notification feed is easy to find. However, if the thought of more notifications on your phone has you shivering, there are ways to keep this inbox quiet.
Where to find Google Wallet's new notification feed
If you have Google Wallet's new notification feed feature, there should be a bell icon next to your profile icon in the top-right of the app. If you click on this bell icon, you'll be brought to the notification feed. This page will be totally blank with a bell in the middle if you have no notifications. Otherwise, you'll find your notifications listed here. Remember, the feed is still being rolled out, so you might not be able to find this page at all.
Any notifications you receive about updates to your saved cards and passes will be stored here. This includes changes to traveling information (such as a gate change on a boarding pass), loyalty and gift cards (like point balance updates), incoming offers and more. This notification feed page will simply aggregate these notifications in one place, allowing you to keep track of them from within the app.
How to manage Google Wallet notifications
One of the reasons you might be happy to see this new notification feed could be rooted in a common problem with Google Wallet, that being the sheer quantity of notifications the app sends. The feed will allow you to find them all in one organized place.
However, depending on your settings, Google Wallet might be taking advantage of Nearby Notifications. Some cards saved to Google Wallet might be sending you offer updates depending on your closeness to a certain location. If you want to avoid notifications from your wallet, this notification feed isn't the thing you want to target. Rather, you want to disable notifications entirely or remove Google's ability to use location data to ping you. You only need to tap on your profile picture, head to Wallet settings > Manage Wallet Notifications and choose the settings you want to tweak. You can also head to Settings > Apps > Google Wallet and either choose Notifications to turn all notifications off or Permissions to deny Google Wallet from using your location.
