title_en: Why your laptop fans spin up without any warning
title_fa: Why your laptop fans spin up without any warning
excerpt_en: Your laptop shouldn't sound like it's preparing for takeoff every time you sit down to work. Here's what might be causing those sudden fan blasts.
excerpt_fa: Your laptop shouldn't sound like it's preparing for takeoff every time you sit down to work. Here's what might be causing those sudden fan blasts.
content_en:
Why your laptop fans spin up without any warning
With a bit of cleaning and system management, you can keep your laptop fan from jump-scaring you.
You're sitting down with your laptop in front of you, getting a bit of light work done, when suddenly you hear what sounds like a jet engine going off. Your computer's fans start roaring and whirring, but after a short moment, everything is quiet again. If you've ever had your laptop fan sound off without warning like this, there are a few possible causes.
Over the years, laptops have become much better at managing performance and cooling, but even the best laptops of today need strong fans to keep their high-powered components cool in such a compact space. While some fan noise is perfectly normal, persistent or unusually loud bursts can indicate that your laptop is working harder than it needs to. Sudden spikes in fan noise are often caused by intensive background activity or dust restricting airflow. Both are relatively easy to investigate, and there are a few simple ways to check what's making your laptop work harder and address the problem.
How to check and clean your laptop fan
The first thing to check if your laptop fan starts acting up is whether it's getting enough airflow. Make sure you're using it on a hard, flat surface like a table or desk rather than a bed, sofa, or other soft surface that could block its vents. If the fan continues to run loudly, dust buildup around the fans or air vents could be the issue.
Luckily, you can typically clean your fans and air vents without taking the machine apart. First, turn off your laptop, unplug any attached devices, and wait for it to cool. Then locate the air vents, which may be on the underside or sides of the device, depending on the model. Use short bursts of compressed air to dislodge dust and debris, following the instructions on the can. You can then wipe away any loose debris with a clean microfiber cloth.
If this approach doesn't do the trick, you may need to dismantle your laptop for greater access to the fans. Along with compressed air, you can also use an ESD-safe brush to remove dust from the components. This process may be a little advanced for some users, and the exact method depends on the type of laptop you're working with. If you're not comfortable taking apart your laptop yourself, it's worth getting in touch with a technician. Also, before dismantling the machine, check your warranty terms and manufacturer's guidance on user repairs, as opening the laptop or carrying out repairs yourself may affect your coverage.
How to check for intensive background activity
If your laptop's fans continue to get extra loud at random intervals, it's possible the CPU is getting a covert workout. On Windows, tap Ctrl+Shift+Esc to open Task Manager and select Processes to see what's running. Click the CPU column to sort processes by how much processing power they're using, putting the biggest resource hogs at the top. Then, head to Startup apps and disable any programs you don't want launching automatically when you start your laptop. If you're a Mac user, open Activity Monitor (hit Command+Spacebar to open Spotlight Search if you're struggling to find it) and head to CPU to identify the processes using the most resources. Click the % CPU column to sort them, then select a process and click the Stop button, then choose Quit.
Before you get trigger-happy, look out for background processes you can live without instead of quitting them willy-nilly (as doing so can lead to some big crashes). On Windows, if you're not using programs like Calculator, Gaming Services, News and Interests, Phone Link, CTF Loader or Groove Music, you can generally end their processes. On Mac, you can quit lingering processes associated with apps you've already closed, Rosetta applications you're no longer using and disk image processes that are preventing a disk from ejecting. You can also disable Spotlight indexing if you don't need your Mac to maintain a fully indexed library.

title_en: Nvidia is investigating Jensen Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy
title_fa: Nvidia is investigating Jensen Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy
excerpt_en: Nvidia has announced that it is opening an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang and his relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who was reportedly recruited by China's Ministry of State Security to spy on the company. A statement posted by the board of directors reads:...
excerpt_fa: Nvidia has announced that it is opening an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang and his relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who was reportedly recruited by China's Ministry of State Security to spy on the company. A statement posted by the board of directors reads:...
content_en:
Nvidia has announced that it is opening an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang and his relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who was reportedly recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on the company. A statement posted by the board of directors reads:
Nvidia is investigating Jensen Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy
Following reports that Nvidia’s CEO had a ‘close relationship’ with an AI exec the company is opening an investigation.
Following reports that Nvidia’s CEO had a ‘close relationship’ with an AI exec the company is opening an investigation.
The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation.
The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders. While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information. Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it.
The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate.
The New York Times reported last month that Huang had developed a “close relationship” with the Megaspeed executive, which he later admitted was romantic in nature in a memo to the company. US officials believe she was feeding information directly back to Beijing.
Megaspeed is a customer of Nvidia and is the subject of a Commerce Department investigation into whether it was smuggling AI chips to China. The company’s AI chips are viewed as crucial to the US maintaining technological supremacy. Both the Biden and Trump administrations have restricted their sale to China. President Trump has loosened those restrictions but still bars sales of Nvidia’s most powerful chips to Chinese firms, and the Commerce Department must approve individual firms to handle the chips.
Just as importantly, Jensen Huang has gotten quite cozy with Donald Trump, and there is concern about what insights into the administration’s deliberations around AI he may have been privy to. And whether any of that information may have been shared with Alice Huang, and eventually found its way to Beijing.

title_en: Don't throw away your old flip phone – do this instead
title_fa: Don't throw away your old flip phone – do this instead
excerpt_en: With smartphones serving all purposes, an old flip phone, especially a SIM-less one, may feel useless. However, this couldn't be further from the truth.
excerpt_fa: With smartphones serving all purposes, an old flip phone, especially a SIM-less one, may feel useless. However, this couldn't be further from the truth.
content_en:
Don't throw away your old flip phone – do this instead
There's plenty you can do with an old flip phone instead of retiring it.
So, you are doing a bit of seasonal cleaning, and you came across the dreaded electronics drawer. One minute you are blissfully tidying up your office, the next you are confronted with a mountainous trove of old gadgets. But don't worry, holding onto an old flip phone is not a surefire sign that you belong on the next episode of "Hoarders."
Despite their lack of advanced features, old cellphones can still serve utilitarian purposes in their old age. From serving as an emergency backup to saving you from crafty pickpockets on vacation, you probably have good reasons to keep your old phones around.
But saving your phone is more than a useful lifehack: It's an ecological imperative. The mass of e-waste mounting in global landfills is an underdiscussed crisis. According to the United Nations' e-Waste Monitor, an estimated 62 million tons of electronics were thrown into the trash heap in 2022, representing an 82% increase from the decade prior. The UN projects yearly e-waste to increase by another 32% by 2030. Containing non-biodegradable materials and toxic chemicals, this mass of e-waste poses an acute danger to our air, water, and soil. Waste from the US alone was found to be causing a "hidden tsunami" of junk in Southeast Asia.
The vast majority of this waste goes unrecycled. According to the UN, less than a quarter of global electronic waste is correctly processed. Luckily, it is easy to recycle your old phone or donate it to charitable organizations in desperate need of cell phones. So if you need to declutter your office, there are an abundance of options that don't involve consigning your device to the global scrap heap.
Repurposing your flip phone
Rather than firing your old flip phone, simply reassign it to a new role. One option is to make your old phone an emergency backup. Notably, this doesn't require you to pay for an active SIM card, either, as all cellular phones in the US can call 911, no matter their carrier status. Keeping an extra phone in your household's emergency response kit will help ensure that you are always able to contact emergency services. Just make sure that it is charged, turned off, and easily accessible in the case of an emergency.
It is important to acknowledge that there are some caveats when using a SIM-less phone in an emergency. When a 911 call is made from an uninitialized phone, dispatchers at the call center are unable to receive critical location information, such as the address from which you called. Moreover, the 911 center won't be able to return your call if you are disconnected. Being aware of these limitations will help you communicate more effectively with first responders.
You can also use a flip phone as a backup dumbphone, which is incredibly useful for instances in which you might damage or lose your smartphone. For instance, dumbphones can be a lifesaver during outdoor activities where your electronics might get wet, such as water sports, fishing trips, or beach days. Longer battery life also makes them a lifesaver during overnight camping trips. Second phones are also helpful when traveling to places where you may have your phone stolen or simply lose it. As a global traveler, having a phone you don't mind losing can be a major luxury when vacationing in crowded cities or events. Unlike your emergency phone, however, you will need a SIM card to swap into your dumb phone as needed.
Donating your phone
If you want to reduce your excess gadgets, there are countless organizations that repurpose used cellphones for a worthy cause. Secure The Call is exemplary of how repurposed gadgets can be used to save lives, providing free 911 emergency phones and tablets to victims of domestic violence, senior citizens, and other high-risk communities. To date, the nonprofit has delivered over 50,000 cellphones to people in need. Other national organizations include More Than A Phone, the 911CellPhoneBank, and Verizon's HopeLine, which operates out of your local Verizon store.
Another notable donation program is Cell Phones For Soldiers, which provides cost-free communication tools and emergency assistance to veterans and active-duty military personnel. Through its Minutes That Matter program, Cell Phones For Soldiers has delivered 8 million prepaid calling cards to active-duty service members overseas, helping them connect with family and friends during difficult deployments. In 2024, the nonprofit began delivering phones to homeless and low-income veterans. In just two years, the nonprofit has delivered 14,500 phones to veterans in need, helping them connect to essential services, loved ones, and potential job opportunities.
Several national organizations help you recycle your used phone and unwanted gadgets, such as The Salvation Army and Goodwill. Large tech chains, like Best Buy and Staples, also offer recycling programs. One helpful resource is the Consumer Technology Association's GreenerGadgets. An online resource aimed at educating consumers about environmental issues, GreenerGadgets has an online search tool to help you find the nearest electronics recycling location. The tool also connects you with mail-back and repair programs. Simply add your zip code and electronic device type to search for a donation center near you. Earth911 is a similar organization that connects you to donation centers with a simple search function.

title_en: Sequoia partners reportedly blindsided when Roelof Botha joined SpaceX board
title_fa: Sequoia partners reportedly blindsided when Roelof Botha joined SpaceX board
excerpt_en: A new report claims Sequoia's recent changes undo the legacy of the firm's former steward.
excerpt_fa: A new report claims Sequoia's recent changes undo the legacy of the firm's former steward.
content_en:
Sequoia Capital announced some major changes this week, including the closure of its London office, the merger of its early-stage and growth teams, and the end of its Scouts program.
Now, the Financial Times has published a report painting all of this as an attempt to undo the legacy of former leader Roelof Botha, who stepped down as the firm’s steward last year. An unnamed source told the FT that Botha “loved process and hierarchy,” while “the rest of the team didn’t.”
Apparently, not everyone is on-board with the changes, with another source firing back that this seems like an “erasure of Sequoia’s heritage, not Roelof’s legacy.”
The break between Botha and his old firm reportedly deepened after Botha joined the SpaceX board this summer. (Botha and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk previously worked together at PayPal.) A source told the FT that Sequoia’s partners were blindsided by the announcement, because Botha “didn’t ask compliance, he didn’t get sign off from the partnership” — even though his new role could complicate the firm’s ability to trade its $20 billion stake.
A Sequoia spokesperson said that the firm continues to “collaborate closely” with Botha.

excerpt_en: Bloomberg's Mark Gurman says CEO John Ternus is pressuring AI czar Craig Federighi to accelerate the Siri roadmap and deliver a powerful AI agent that can compete with OpenAI's Dots or Meta's Muse. While Federighi has delivered a functional version of Siri AI on an incredibly...
excerpt_fa: Bloomberg's Mark Gurman says CEO John Ternus is pressuring AI czar Craig Federighi to accelerate the Siri roadmap and deliver a powerful AI agent that can compete with OpenAI's Dots or Meta's Muse. While Federighi has delivered a functional version of Siri AI on an incredibly...
content_en:
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman says CEO John Ternus is pressuring AI czar Craig Federighi to accelerate the Siri roadmap and deliver a powerful AI agent that can compete with OpenAI’s Dots or Meta’s Muse. While Federighi has delivered a functional version of Siri AI on an incredibly short timeline, the company has no illusions that it’s keeping pace with its rivals.
Apple is racing to make Siri more agentic
Future versions of Siri will be able to control third-party apps and perform more complex tasks.
Future versions of Siri will be able to control third-party apps and perform more complex tasks.
Two significant improvements are expected to be made to Siri in the coming months. One will give the assistant fine-grained control over Apple’s first-party apps, allowing it to do things like rotate and crop images in Photos and organize Safari tabs. Those capabilities are expected to land with iOS 27.3. The bigger change, integration with third-party apps, is likely to land later, in the Spring, according to Gurman. That would let Siri place an order through Grubhub or book a dinner reservation through OpenTable, for example.
But that’s just the start. Apple is expected to push Siri to become more agentic and enable features that will allow it to perform ongoing tasks, not just one-offs. Gurman says:
Dots, Muse and Grok can keep track of goals, determine what needs to happen next and continue pursuing objectives without the user initiating every individual step. Apple ultimately wants to go in this direction, I’m told, and I believe the company could make Siri more like an agent as early as next year — not that it has much of a choice, given current consumer and market demands.

title_en: SNL has a new impression of Elon Musk, ‘the worst thing South Africa has ever done’
title_fa: SNL has a new impression of Elon Musk, ‘the worst thing South Africa has ever done’
excerpt_en: SNL seems to have its knives out for tech executives.
excerpt_fa: SNL seems to have its knives out for tech executives.
content_en:
Saturday Night Live cast member Jeremy Culhane unveiled his impression of Elon Musk last night, depicting the SpaceX and Tesla CEO as an awkward loser who fumbles his attempt to befriend the hosts of Weekend Update.
This isn’t the first time the show has lampooned the world’s richest man (and one-time SNL host), with Mike Myers dropping by occasionally to wield a chainsaw before freezing and muttering, “Glitch!”
Since Musk was in the news this week for spending half a billion dollars on candidates who lost in the midterms, then announcing plans to halt Cybertruck production, it’s maybe not surprising that Culhane’s version is a little less obnoxious and a little more desperate to be liked, doing his best to laugh off his setbacks and remind the audience, “My car did a flip!”
Eventually, Weekend Update co-host Colin Jost asks a pointed question about Musk’s week: “You moved to Texas because California was run by Democrats. You moved all your companies to Texas because you didn’t want to pay taxes. You even built your own town in Texas. And now Texas is run by Democrats. Now you’re going to have to pay taxes. So how does that make you feel?”
Culhane nods along with each step of the question, then answers, “Bad?”
To show that he’s a good sport about all this, Culhane also asks his chatbot Grok to do “an epic vulgar roast of me, Elon Musk.” Grok delivers, describing Musk as “the worst thing South Africa has ever done” and suggesting, “Maybe if you have 100 more kids, one of them will talk to you.”
This week’s episode also featured a spoof of the Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything,” featuring Jane Wickline’s uncanny take on the Theranos founder (though most of the jokes focus on episode host Druski).
SNL seems to have its knives out for tech executives this season, starting with Wickline’s impression of Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei as a stuttering prophet of AI doom.
A couple weeks later, James Austin Johnson caricatured data center backer/”Marty Supreme” co-star Kevin O’Leary. Asked about the widespread public opposition to data centers, Johnson-as-O’Leary smoothly replies, “All I want is to buy up 40,000 acres of God’s untouched splendor and replace it with a very loud computer that steals your job.”

title_en: Elvis and Eminem rights holders are suing Suno
title_fa: Elvis and Eminem rights holders are suing Suno
excerpt_en: Suno is facing yet another pair of lawsuits. A group of rights holders of Elvis Presley's music and the publisher of some of Eminem's biggest records are suing the AI music company, claiming it illegally generates music and lyrics that mimic those artists. The lawyers in the...
excerpt_fa: Suno is facing yet another pair of lawsuits. A group of rights holders of Elvis Presley's music and the publisher of some of Eminem's biggest records are suing the AI music company, claiming it illegally generates music and lyrics that mimic those artists. The lawyers in the...
content_en:
Suno is facing yet another pair of lawsuits. A group of rights holders of Elvis Presley’s music and the publisher of some of Eminem‘s biggest records are suing the AI music company, claiming it illegally generates music and lyrics that mimic those artists. The lawyers in the Presley suit claim that Suno has violated Tennessee’s Ensuring Likeness Voice and Image Security (ELVIS) Act, which makes it illegal for an AI company to clone a singer’s voice.
Elvis and Eminem rights holders are suing Suno
Suno is facing two more lawsuits over AI music clones.
Suno is facing two more lawsuits over AI music clones.
In the suit, lawyers representing Presley’s rights holders argue that “Suno has mechanically encoded itself with artists’ identities, hard-work, creativity, and time, and harnessed them all for a consistent conveyor belt of
cold hard cash.“ These suits closely mirror one filed by Jason Isbell and others in September, which claimed Suno created imitations of the plaintiffs but did not claim copyright infringement directly.
Later in the complaint, the lawyers write that “Suno’s ravenous race to the bottom aims to make human creativity obsolete, coldly replicating without a license in seconds what takes years to learn, struggle with, maintain, and endlessly attempt to make better and perfect.”
Suno spokesperson Cat McCormack told The Verge that, “Suno exists to help people create new, original music, not to trade on anyone’s name or likeness, and we prohibit any unauthorized use of an artist’s work. To protect against this, we do not allow prompts for specific artists’ names and songs and work with third-party providers to screen uploaded audio files and lyrics for potential misuse. We are always working to strengthen our guardrails and we will continue to add new safeguards that protect artists and our users.”
This adds to the pile of lawsuits Suno is currently facing from Sony, UMG, Isbell, Reservoir Media, and more.

title_en: TechCrunch Mobility: The Cybertruck experiment is over
title_fa: TechCrunch Mobility: The Cybertruck experiment is over
excerpt_en: Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it.
excerpt_fa: Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it.
content_en:
Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility!
Almost seven years ago, while clutching a laptop, my phone, and a notebook in a sea of Tesla fans, I watched head designer Franz von Holzhausen throw a metal, baseball-sized ball at the driver’s-side window of the Cybertruck. The result was cracked glass — actually, two by the end of the presentation — and some awkward jokes and chuckling by CEO Elon Musk.
I have witnessed a number of stunning, odd, and fantastical moments at Tesla events. But the Cybertruck reveal was the most interesting — and not because of the postapocalyptic design. It was the crowd.
When the truck rolled out onto the stage, I watched attendees gasp, some in revulsion. There was mumbling (“This certainly can’t be the Cybertruck?” I heard Tesla superfans whisper). And yes, there were cheers. The momentary shock of Musk’s biggest fans was quickly replaced by support, acceptance, and finally, endorsement.
It moved like a wave over the crowd. By the time attendees were waiting in line for Cybertruck rides, the mood had shifted. Everyone was a fan.
That fandom carried over to Cybertruck reservations, which skyrocketed to 1 million, Musk said during a third-quarter earnings call in 2023. But it never made the leap to actual sales. Industry experts estimate about 71,000 Cybertrucks have been sold since the first deliveries began in November 2023.
And now the Cybertruck is headed to the scrap pile. Tesla will stop making the Cybertruck next year, Musk said Friday.
Was the vehicle too edgy? Maybe, but this was always going to be a niche market. I believe more practical reasons dampened sales. Musk promised the Cybertruck would have a 500-mile range and a price tag under $40,000. It achieved neither, senior reporter Sean O’Kane noted in his report.
Deals!
Zipline has had quite the week. Strike that — quite the year. The autonomous drone delivery startup, which was founded in 2014, has steadily scaled over the past few years. But 2026 has taken the company to new heights.
In early 2026, Zipline raised $600 million and quickly added another $200 million to that Series H round. The company planned to use these funds to accelerate its expansion to at least four U.S. cities in 2026.
Now it has even more money to grow even faster. Zipline announced this week it raised $1.5 billion and ramped up its partnership with Walmart to add 300 drone delivery sites across the United States. Zipline is now valued at $21.5 billion.
Other deals that got my attention …
Electric truck startup Harbinger raised a $240 million Series D funding round as it expands its portfolio of products, including battery storage and defense applications. No word on the company’s valuation.
Humble Robotics raised $51 million in a Series A round, bringing total funding to $75 million less than a year after founding. The round was led by Obvious Ventures with participation from insiders Eclipse, Energy Impact Partners, and others.
Static Media acquired automotive news site CarScoops, adding to its existing portfolio that includes 34 brands such as Engadget, Jalopnik, and SlashGear.
Notable reads and other tidbits
Also, the micromobility startup spun out of Rivian in 2025, quietly started and then walked away from an electric two-wheeler pilot project in Kenya earlier this year, as it sought to focus its resources on its consumer e-bike and autonomous vehicle ambitions.
Amazon has made Uber Eats its official restaurant delivery partner for Prime members in the United States, effectively ending the e-commerce giant’s existing deal with Grubhub.
The Luce, Ferrari’s first electric car and one of its most polarizing models, is “fully allocated” for 2027.
Ford unveiled what it’s calling a “privacy promise” — an “explicit commitment” to keep customers’ vehicle data safe and give them control over what they share. Ford also launched a website designed to educate customers about how, where, and why the automaker uses their data, and to show them how to change those settings.
May Mobility and Forterra advanced to phase three of the Department of Defense’s Robotic Operations for Autonomous Delivery and Sustainment (ROADS) prize challenge, an initiative to test and adopt commercial self-driving vehicles in the military.
Serve Robotics announced plans to launch a new business line called Physical AI Services. The company will still operate and expand its autonomous delivery operations and become a technology supplier to other companies building robots.
The predictions of AI agents booking restaurants, trips, and even rides for the masses hasn’t quite materialized yet. Uber reported during its third-quarter earnings call that only four rides were ordered through an AI agent during its busiest week in October: the week of Halloween.
Waymo is shaking up its Uber relationship, confirming months of speculation. The company will end its exclusivity with Uber in the Austin and Atlanta markets starting in January 2028.
One more thing …
Over the past three years, this newsletter often highlighted an investigation, scoop, or interview from senior reporter Sean O’Kane. Some of my favorites were the articles we collaborated on, including his scoop that Jeff Bezos was backing Slate Auto, our story about how Jony Ive’s LoveFrom had worked on the design of the Also e-bike, his investigation into Fisker, and his coverage of how Waymo was relying on first responders to help move its robotaxis.
We have co-bylined dozens of articles on company earnings and breaking news and co-hosted Equity, TechCrunch’s flagship podcast about the business of startups. And so it’s bittersweet to see him head off on a new adventure at the Wall Street Journal to cover Tesla.
Congrats on the gig, Sean! We hate to see you go!
I will, of course, continue to deliver readers insider details, scoops, and...

Industry experts estimate about 71,000 Cybertrucks have been sold since the first deliveries began in November 2023.
And now the Cybertruck is headed to the scrap pile. Tesla will stop making the Cybertruck next year, Musk said Friday.
Was the vehicle too edgy? Maybe, but this was always going to be a niche market. I believe more practical reasons dampened sales. Musk promised the Cybertruck would have a 500-mile range and a price tag under $40,000. It achieved neither, senior reporter Sean O’Kane noted in his report.
Deals!
Zipline has had quite the week. Strike that — quite the year. The autonomous drone delivery startup, which was founded in 2014, has steadily scaled over the past few years. But 2026 has taken the company to new heights.
In early 2026, Zipline raised $600 million and quickly added another $200 million to that Series H round. The company planned to use these funds to accelerate its expansion to at least four U.S. cities in 2026.
Now it has even more money to grow even faster. Zipline announced this week it raised $1.5 billion and ramped up its partnership with Walmart to add 300 drone delivery sites across the United States. Zipline is now valued at $21.5 billion.
Other deals that got my attention …
Electric truck startup Harbinger raised a $240 million Series D funding round as it expands its portfolio of products, including battery storage and defense applications. No word on the company’s valuation.
Humble Robotics raised $51 million in a Series A round, bringing total funding to $75 million less than a year after founding. The round was led by Obvious Ventures with participation from insiders Eclipse, Energy Impact Partners, and others.
Static Media acquired automotive news site CarScoops, adding to its existing portfolio that includes 34 brands such as Engadget, Jalopnik, and SlashGear.
Notable reads and other tidbits
Also, the micromobility startup spun out of Rivian in 2025, quietly started and then walked away from an electric two-wheeler pilot project in Kenya earlier this year, as it sought to focus its resources on its consumer e-bike and autonomous vehicle ambitions.
Amazon has made Uber Eats its official restaurant delivery partner for Prime members in the United States, effectively ending the e-commerce giant’s existing deal with Grubhub.
The Luce, Ferrari’s first electric car and one of its most polarizing models, is “fully allocated” for 2027.
Ford unveiled what it’s calling a “privacy promise” — an “explicit commitment” to keep customers’ vehicle data safe and give them control over what they share. Ford also launched a website designed to educate customers about how, where, and why the automaker uses their data, and to show them how to change those settings.
May Mobility and Forterra advanced to phase three of the Department of Defense’s Robotic Operations for Autonomous Delivery and Sustainment (ROADS) prize challenge, an initiative to test and adopt commercial self-driving vehicles in the military.
Serve Robotics announced plans to launch a new business line called Physical AI Services. The company will still operate and expand its autonomous delivery operations and become a technology supplier to other companies building robots.
The predictions of AI agents booking restaurants, trips, and even rides for the masses hasn’t quite materialized yet. Uber reported during its third-quarter earnings call that only four rides were ordered through an AI agent during its busiest week in October: the week of Halloween.
Waymo is shaking up its Uber relationship, confirming months of speculation. The company will end its exclusivity with Uber in the Austin and Atlanta markets starting in January 2028.
One more thing …
Over the past three years, this newsletter often highlighted an investigation, scoop, or interview from senior reporter Sean O’Kane. Some of my favorites were the articles we collaborated on, including his scoop that Jeff Bezos was backing Slate Auto, our story about how Jony Ive’s LoveFrom had worked on the design of the Also e-bike, his investigation into Fisker, and his coverage of how Waymo was relying on first responders to help move its robotaxis.
We have co-bylined dozens of articles on company earnings and breaking news and co-hosted Equity, TechCrunch’s flagship podcast about the business of startups. And so it’s bittersweet to see him head off on a new adventure at the Wall Street Journal to cover Tesla.
Congrats on the gig, Sean! We hate to see you go!

title_en: Apple’s M5 MacBook Air is down to its lowest price since July
title_fa: Apple’s M5 MacBook Air is down to its lowest price since July
excerpt_en: The latest 13-inch MacBook Air is currently available for $1,099.99, marking the second time we’ve seen this $200 discount following the company’s hefty price increases over the summer. Although the base model — which features Apple’s M5 processor, 16GB of RAM, and 512GB of...
excerpt_fa: The latest 13-inch MacBook Air is currently available for $1,099.99, marking the second time we’ve seen this $200 discount following the company’s hefty price increases over the summer. Although the base model — which features Apple’s M5 processor, 16GB of RAM, and 512GB of...
content_en:
The latest 13-inch MacBook Air is currently available for $1,099.99, marking the second time we’ve seen this $200 discount following the company’s hefty price increases over the summer. Although the base model — which features Apple’s M5 processor, 16GB of RAM, and 512GB of storage — often sold for around $950 to $1,000 shortly after it launched in May, savings have been rare since July, making the current deal worth flagging. Amazon, Best Buy, and B&H Photo are all honoring the price across all color options.
Apple’s M5 MacBook Air is down to its lowest price since July
You can get a temporary break from the $200 price hike that hit both Air sizes this summer.
You can get a temporary break from the $200 price hike that hit both Air sizes this summer.
If you’d prefer something with a larger screen, a six-speaker array instead of four, and slightly more power (with two additional GPU cores in the M5), Apple’s 15-inch MacBook Air is also on sale for $200 off. Amazon, Best Buy, and B&H Photo are each selling the 16GB RAM / 512GB SSD configuration in most colors for $1,299.99.
Apple 13-inch MacBook Air (M5)
Although it’s pricier than the newer MacBook Neo, the Air offers better value in numerous ways. It’s an ideal choice if you want faster performance, as it offers double the RAM and a speedier CPU with more cores. You also get twice as much storage, better speakers, a backlit keyboard, and a larger, higher-resolution screen. Given said differences, it’s easy to see how the Air’s improvements might make it worth the extra cost for some people.
If you’re still on the fence, though, I’d recommend reading my colleague Antonio G. Di Benedetto’s reviews, both of which were published before the summer price increases.

content_en:
Code in the iOS 27.3 beta suggests that Apple could add support for chatbots to its smart home hub. There’s a flag listed for a “Conversational Apps” category. While there are no details about what apps would fall under that heading, it seems reasonable that AI chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude could be added to HomeView. According to pdfu on X, that new beta also adds support for bidirectional audio routing and session management, but says it’s “still not fully wired up.”
Chatbots might be coming to Apple’s HomeView
Code in iOS 27.3 has a flag for ‘Conversational Apps.’
Code in iOS 27.3 has a flag for ‘Conversational Apps.’
Apple has also added anti-spoofing protection that will require a user to authenticate themselves with an iPhone after three failed attempts. It will also have a lockout system with increasingly longer wait times, starting at one hour for the second lockout, and climbing to eight for the fourth.
Neither feature has been officially announced by Apple, and there’s no word on when they might become available.

title_en: Ninja’s AutoBarista is impressively versatile, but one feature was a dealbreaker for me
title_fa: Ninja’s AutoBarista is impressively versatile, but one feature was a dealbreaker for me
excerpt_en: The AutoBarista's "Grind iQ" technology allows the machine to analyze your coffee beans to inform how it pulls a shot of espresso.
excerpt_fa: The AutoBarista's "Grind iQ" technology allows the machine to analyze your coffee beans to inform how it pulls a shot of espresso.
content_en:
I’ve made about a dozen different kinds of coffee drinks with the Ninja AutoBarista, and I have absolutely no idea what sort of grind size, tamping pressure, water temperature, or extraction timing is necessary to pull espresso shots for any of those drinks. The AutoBarista takes care of these considerations for you, making it possible to brew 13 different drinks with just the press of a button.
The AutoBarista seeks to create the experience of having a coffee shop inside of your home, but without having to master the complicated, time-consuming nuances of making perfect espresso. It makes drip coffee and espresso-and-milk drinks, like cappuccinos or flat white. The fully automatic espresso machine can even make a pretty fast cold brew or cold-pressed espresso (just add ice, or else it’s more like lukewarm brew).
The AutoBarista’s versatility comes from its “Grind iQ” feature. This technology allows the machine to pick up on your coffee bean size, roast type, and freshness, auto-calibrating the grind size, weight, and dose of each brew to make your drink of choice. As you customize the number of shots in your drink, the intensity of the shot, and the temperature, Grind iQ adjusts as well.
If using something like Grind iQ sounds like bowling with the bumpers up, or playing Mario Kart with steer assist, then this is not a machine for you — stick with your pour overs and enjoy your gooseneck electric kettle. This is not a machine for coffee snobs who want to control every last detail of the brewing process. Rather, it’s for people who love coffee, but have never analyzed their espresso pucks.
With the caveat that I am not invested in the coffee brewing process, I will say that I think the AutoBarista makes good drinks.
On one side of the machine, it can pull shots of espresso or brew drip coffee, while on the other, it has an automatic milk frother and stainless steel pitcher, which allows you to customize settings based on your desired temperature and heaviness of the foam. It also includes a setting for frothing plant-based milk.
To keep the coffee tasting good, the AutoBarista always rinses itself before and after making a drink. This is a useful feature — I often find myself manually running water through my Nespresso machine, since I don’t use it every day. But the water catches in a drip tray, which fills up after making just a few drinks, so if you live with another person, then emptying the tray will be a daily nuisance. While the design of the machine makes it easy to pull out the tray, I’ve accidentally overfilled it and spilled coffee-tinted water on my kitchen floor more than once. That’s the dealbreaker.
When you pull out the drip tray, you’ll also see the knock box, which collects your spent espresso pucks. Be warned: if you forget to empty the knock box for even just a few days, you may get jump-scared by some blue mold next time you go to dump the pucks. Maybe I should’ve seen that coming, but scrubbing the moldy knock box made me feel ready to go back to my beloved OXO Cold Brew Coffee Maker, which costs just six percent of the price of the AutoBarista.
In the AutoBarista’s defense, most people probably wouldn’t find this machine so arduous to care for. I just happen to be someone who makes one big batch cold brew every other week and tries to keep my morning rituals minimal. If you have more patience than I do before 8 AM, then you may very well love this machine and find it low maintenance.
Ninja excels at making multi-use kitchen products, and the AutoBarista is no exception, combining a drip coffee maker, espresso machine, milk frother, and grinder, and food scale into one device. But if you’re not planning to take advantage of the AutoBarista’s versatility, then it’s not worth paying its $999.99 price.

content_en:
This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on the pressures of creating content for the internet, follow Mia Sato. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.
There’s no slowing down media’s pivot-to-video 2.0
Just as publishers are starting to crack the vertical video code, social media platforms are looking ahead to a new format.
There’s no slowing down media’s pivot-to-video 2.0
Just as publishers are starting to crack the vertical video code, social media platforms are looking ahead to a new format.
How it started
Almost exactly a decade ago, the media industry was in the middle of a video revolution — or so it thought. In the mid-2010s, publications poured money into burgeoning social media video efforts, chasing the promise of reaching larger audiences and opening new lines of revenue. Print publications and digital news outlets alike hired teams, pumped out content, and entrusted platforms like Facebook with their reach and distribution.
That pivot-to-video slowly revealed itself to be a lot of smoke and mirrors when it became clear that Facebook had inflated video views. Newsrooms cut writers and editors in a move to video — and then cut those video teams when they realized the pivot had not paid off. For many in the media industry, social video brings to mind layoffs and instability rather than the promised abundance.
A “pivot” feels inadequate to describe the current emphasis on social video, not just in newsrooms but in society writ large. Social media companies have reorganized their feeds to emphasize video, spurred by the massive growth of TikTok during the pandemic. But the media industry is still playing catch-up, and in some cases it seems to have been slow to jump in (perhaps cautious given past experience). It took years for some publishers to start incorporating vertical video on their websites, apps, and stories, for example, and it takes coordination and intention to get individual reporters in front of a camera to talk about their work. In the meantime, YouTube has become the most popular streamer, commanding nearly 16 percent of TV viewing, according to Nielsen. Twenty percent of Americans regularly get news from TikTok, and that number jumps to 39 percent for people 18 to 29 years old, Pew found.
Viewers favor the stripped-down selfie-style video dispatches from personalities they trust, even if those creators are not themselves reporting and writing the news. Compared with a decade ago, the barrier to entry and cost of making video content has plummeted: Anyone with a smartphone can become a video creator, no fancy equipment or editing needed. Social video is fast, personality-driven, casual, and, at times, unfiltered — the exact opposite from what news outlets are used to. A second pivot-to-video is underway, and the media industry once again wants in.
How it’s going
Video is unavoidable on social media, if not an expected part of how people and institutions show up online. TikTok’s influence is felt everywhere: on competitor platforms like Meta’s Reels and YouTube Shorts, of course, but also in unexpected places, like LinkedIn. There are no signs of it slowing down, either: The time spent watching Reels on Facebook was at an all-time high in Q3. Early tests in other countries suggest Meta is toying with the idea of dropping users directly into full-screen video upon opening the Instagram and Facebook apps. The appetite for video seems insatiable, and if news organizations won’t lean in, armies of content creators will be happy to scoop up the audiences.
Some news outlets were relatively early to the short-form social video boom. The Washington Post, for example, found notable success on TikTok before many peers had even created dedicated accounts on the platform. (Dave Jorgenson, the face of the Post’s social video effort, left the paper last year. He now makes short and longform videos under Local News International — perhaps a testament to the trust that viewers place in individual creators.)
Beyond having a short-form video presence, some traditional news outlets are leaning into formats and styles popularized in the vertical video era. CNN partnered with Jubilee, the popular channel that produces debate-me-style videos on hot-button political topics. The CNN town hall with Texas Senate candidate James Talarico was conducted in the Jubilee style. The New York Times, which for years has produced polished documentary-style videos, recently introduced the vertical video series “The Call.” Unlike the Times’ more buttoned-up videos, the point of “The Call” is to create a sense of intimacy, like you’re getting updates from a friend: The show’s host ostensibly makes a video call to a journalist reporting on the ground to ask them about what they’re witnessing.
News outlets are also directly hiring or working with content creators. Some outlets like The Washington Post have spun up so-called creator networks, where they partner with influencers to produce content independent from the newsroom. A new program supported by Poynter and Microsoft pairs content creators with a handful of news outlets so they can create content tailored for social media.
And then, of course, there are the clips. Podcasts became videos, which became bite-sized clips of podcasts formatted for vertical feeds. TV shows became web shows, which gave rise to microdramas. News articles — even major investigations — are now adapted for vertical video audiences. Individual reporters (myself included) make talking-head clips explaining our reporting. Earlier this year, I called this phenomenon “the clippening”: the reformatting of all media to be legible in a vertical video feed, even if the original work is neither vertical nor video. It’s hard to fault the people and institutions putting resources into social video — audiences are consuming it — but it’s also feeling a lot like...

title_en: Syncing Apple Music across your devices is easier than you think
title_fa: Syncing Apple Music across your devices is easier than you think
excerpt_en: One perk of subscribing to Apple Music is having your collection synced across all your devices - and all it takes is a simple toggle. Here's how.
excerpt_fa: One perk of subscribing to Apple Music is having your collection synced across all your devices - and all it takes is a simple toggle. Here's how.
content_en:
Syncing Apple Music across your devices is easier than you think
Using Apple Music on multiple devices? Keeping them in sync is a breeze.
Apple Music is one of the best music streaming platforms right now, especially for Apple device owners. But despite its association with the tech giant, Apple Music is not exclusive to Apple devices and is available on multiple platforms. You can, for example, sign in with your Apple Account and listen to your favorite songs on an Android phone, Windows PC or even smart TVs.
After signing in on a new device, though, you may notice that your music library isn't synced and your songs aren't there. If this has happened to you, don't worry. Changing a single setting in Apple Music will prompt it to sync your music across all your devices, ensuring you don't have to manage your library manually on each one.
How to turn on Sync Library on Apple Music
The main reason Apple Music might not sync your library across devices is that you're using different accounts on each device, so check that first. If you're not sure which account you're using, open the Apple Music app and tap your profile picture on the Home tab. Now make sure Sync Library is enabled on your devices. On your iPhone or iPad, open Settings and look for Apps. Then, find the Music app in the list and enable Sync Library. Now, under the General tab, make sure Sync Library is enabled and click OK to save your settings. The process is pretty much the same in Windows, but you need to click the three-dot button instead to find Settings. If you have an Android phone, this option is enabled by default, and you don't need to change anything.
No matter the platform, the first sync might take a while, especially if you have a large music library. If you don't see your songs right away after enabling syncing, leave the Music app open and wait a few minutes.
What to do when Apple Music won't sync
In the Mac app, click the File menu, then go to Library and select Update Cloud Library — this will force the app to sync and check for updates in your personal library. This option is also available in the Windows app and can be found in the sidebar. Unfortunately, the Android and iOS apps don't have that option.
Also, make sure your mobile devices are connected to Wi-Fi and not in Low Power Mode, as this may prevent them from syncing your music library. If nothing else has worked, your best option is to go back to Settings, turn off Sync Library and then turn it back on. You can also try signing out of your Apple Account and logging back in. If you don't subscribe to Apple Music and have an offline library on your Mac or PC, the only way to sync your library is to manually transfer the Music folder to another computer via Apple iTunes or Apple Devices.
Syncing behavior isn't the only setting you might want to change in Apple Music. While you're there, it's worth exploring some other toggles, like changing the audio quality options to enable lossless audio.

title_en: Samsung One UI 9.5 beta may be coming soon: Here's how to sign up for the program
title_fa: Samsung One UI 9.5 beta may be coming soon: Here's how to sign up for the program
excerpt_en: Samsung appears to be preparing the One UI 9.5 beta program ahead of an expected 2027 launch. Here's what to do if you want to test Samsung's latest OS.
excerpt_fa: Samsung appears to be preparing the One UI 9.5 beta program ahead of an expected 2027 launch. Here's what to do if you want to test Samsung's latest OS.
content_en:
Samsung One UI 9.5 beta may be coming soon: Here's how to sign up for the program
Beta firmware for the Galaxy S26 Ultra is already on Samsung's servers.
If you've been aggressively refreshing the Samsung Members app on your Galaxy S26 in the hope of seeing the One UI 9.5 beta, you're wasting your time — although you won't have to wait much longer. A One UI 9.5 beta build for the Galaxy S26 Ultra has appeared on Samsung's Korean and US update servers, which is typically the last step before the company opens registrations.
Samsung hasn't announced the beta or a launch date, but its last point-five update, One UI 8.5, opened to testers on December 8 2025. One UI 9.5 is expected to launch with the Galaxy S27 early in 2027, so a beta release is definitely imminent. If you're interested, signing up will work the same way as last time: register in Samsung Members, then download the beta from your phone's settings once it's available. That is, provided you live in one of six countries — Germany, India, Poland, South Korea, the UK or the US — and own the right phone.
The build that's been spotted is firmware version S948BXXU6ZZK3, and it's for the S26 Ultra only, though other S26 phones and servers will almost certainly get the beta. Enthusiast site SammyGuru also expects the S25 series, Z Fold 8 and Z Flip 8 to get the beta as well. Even if you have an S26, though, you may miss out if you bought it through a carrier. The One UI 8.5 beta was only available for unlocked phones in the US, and users with a carrier-locked S26 will probably have to wait for the stable release.
When the beta is likely to open
Samsung opened the One UI 8.5 beta on December 8, 2025, for the Galaxy S25, S25+ and S25 Ultra, but not everyone got it on day one: Owners in Poland and India had to wait until the second beta build on December 22. Samsung launched One UI 8.5 on the Galaxy S26 at its February 2026 Unpacked event, and released a beta for the Galaxy S24 series, Z Fold 6, Z Flip 6, S25 FE, S24 FE and Galaxy Tab S11 in late March.
The One UI 9.0 beta rolled out on May 13, and the stable version released with the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Z Flip 8 on July 22, in step with Google's Android 17 release. One UI 9.5 is still based on Android 17, putting it in the same mid-cycle slot 8.5 filled last year and timed for the next Galaxy S phones. As of writing, Samsung hasn't announced a date for the S27's Unpacked event, though it'll probably mirror recent years and fall somewhere in January or February.
Enthusiast site SammyFans has pencilled in early December for the beta, while SamMobile thinks registrations could open in November. Both sites are working from a single previous point-five release, though; the S26's Ultra build sitting on Samsung's servers is a far better indication that a beta is imminent.
How to sign up
To sign up for the beta, you'll need a Samsung account and the Samsung Members app, which you can download from the Galaxy Store or Google Play. Once the beta itself goes live, you'll simply need to open Samsung Members, tap the One UI 9.5 banner or beta card on the home screen and select Registration for One UI Beta Program. If your phone and country qualify, Samsung will enrol you. From there, head to Settings > Software update > Download and install to get the beta. Samsung rolls builds out gradually, so don't panic if it doesn't show up immediately.
Before installing the beta, you should update all your apps and back up your phone to a computer with Smart Switch, since beta software can corrupt your data. If you come across any bugs, you can report them through Samsung Members > Participated Beta test > Beta feedback > Send feedback.
Exiting the beta is the more awkward part. You can withdraw by navigating via Samsung Members > Settings > Beta program settings > Withdraw from beta program, but that doesn't remove the beta build itself. Instead, you'll need to plug your phone into a computer and use Smart Switch to run a Downgrade, which will wipe everything you've done during testing. If you choose to stay on the beta, you'll get the finished One UI 9.5 as a normal update, whenever that is. So, if your S26 is your only phone and you don't keep regular backups, it's worth sitting this one out and waiting for the stable release.

title_en: How do spam callers get your number in the first place?
title_fa: How do spam callers get your number in the first place?
excerpt_en: Ever wonder how a total stranger ended up with your phone number? The answer starts earlier than you think, and a few small habits can keep it from spreading.
excerpt_fa: Ever wonder how a total stranger ended up with your phone number? The answer starts earlier than you think, and a few small habits can keep it from spreading.
content_en:
How do spam callers get your number in the first place?
Spam calls getting you down? Here's how robocallers got your number in the first place.
Whether it's spam calls or text messages, the modern world is dominated by flooded inboxes and phone scams. If you find yourself inundated with notifications about packages you didn't order or services you've never used, you might wonder how all these ads and cons made their way to you. Luckily, you can stem the flow of slop.
There are many ways to stop spam calls on Android, iPhone and other devices, but an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure. If you want to get ahead of spammers, you need to know how you're getting spammed in the first place.
Unfortunately, many of these causes are out of your hands, such as random robocaller dials and data breaches. On the bright side, there are some steps you can take to keep your number from spreading further.
How spam callers get your number
A good portion of spam calls and texts come from sheer bad luck. Sometimes you need to use your number for an important account, only for that site or service to be hit by a data breach. Either that, or an illegal robocaller has randomly dialed your number or stolen it from a public record, like a court directory, property deeds or corporate filings.
Even if you're registered with the FTC's Do Not Call Registry, which restricts most telemarketing calls, you can still be spammed by charities, political parties, debt collectors, telephone surveyors and other exempt callers.
The bulk of numbers available to spammers and scammers, however, have been bought from data brokers. In many cases, this data is legally resold to third parties after you sign up for accounts, loyalty programs, contests, sweepstakes and more. You probably agreed to these sales, either as a mandatory condition of using a service or while rushing through web pages with deliberately confusing checkboxes.
You may also have fallen victim to a phishing scam, handing over your information by filling out a fake login page, making an account on a sketchy website, applying to a fake job listing or signing up for a bogus app or service. If you've signed up for anything with your phone number, there's a strong likelihood your information has been sold.
How to keep your phone number safe
Your devices do have a level of protection against phishing, from browser warnings about risk sites to Android's enhanced protection against bank scams. But there are also ways to take precautions with your number.
Always keep an eye on the sites you use and avoid ones that are stuffed with ads or that you don't recognize. You can be extra safe by searching for reviews and scam reports about a site before you sign up. In general, though, hide your number on any public profiles and be mindful of how many accounts you create and which boxes you check.
If you're under attack from robocallers who just won't stop, signing up for the FTC's registry is one way to limit your risk. If you want to find out how your number may have gotten out, check whether an associated account was part of a data breach by searching your email address on a site like Have I Been Pwned. You can also google your own phone number in quotes to see if it pops up anywhere.

title_en: What does Apple One Family come with and which subscription is best for you?
title_fa: What does Apple One Family come with and which subscription is best for you?
excerpt_en: Apple One offers strong value if you're using a lot of Apple services anyway, but make sure you do the math before signing up.
excerpt_fa: Apple One offers strong value if you're using a lot of Apple services anyway, but make sure you do the math before signing up.
content_en:
What does Apple One Family come with and which subscription is best for you?
The answer comes down to how many of Apple's services you use regularly.
This year, several of Apple's subscriptions saw serious price upticks, so much so that even students had to pay a bit more. Apple Music prices rose by $1 a month for individual plans and $3 for the Family plan. A few weeks later, monthly Apple TV subscriptions went up from $13 to 15, while annual ones saw a $20 total jump.
If you use many Apple services, you might have looked to Apple One to bundle them and reduce the hurt from these increases. Unfortunately, the package subscription didn't get by unscathed either. The Individual tier climbed from $20 to $22 a month, though it's still cheaper than subscribing to Apple Music ($12/month) and Apple TV ($15/month) separately.
While the Apple One Family plan is now $28/month, you can share it with five other people, which drastically brings down the cost per person. There's also a higher-cost shareable Premier tier at $40/month. But before you ask friends and family to group up with you, you need to figure out which of the three Apple One subscriptions is most worth your while. That mostly depends on how many Apple services you already use.
Which Apple One tier makes the most sense for you?
Getting the cheapest tier out of the way: Individual subscribers get Apple TV, Apple Music, Apple Arcade and 50GB of iCloud storage for $22 per month; that's about $13 less than it would be to subscribe to each one on its own.
Moving on, the Family tier is a great choice if you're providing for multiple people or want to split the monthly cost with up to five other members. At $28 per month, you get a shared 200GB pool of iCloud storage, the Apple Music Family plan (which costs $20 by itself), plus Apple TV and Apple Arcade. Combined, the Family plan saves you about $17 per month, which can stretch even further if you split the bill. With six people paying their own way, each person pays less than $5/month. Unlike some family plans, Apple doesn't require everyone to live in the same household.
The final step up is Apple One Premier, which offers the full suite of Apple services and $35 in monthly savings compared to joining each one individually. Along with everything included in the Family plan, you also get Apple Fitness+ ($10 per month), Apple News+ ($13/month) and 2TB of shared iCloud storage ($10 per month). On their own, these would total $75, so it's a good value at $40 per month.
Before deciding, you need to narrow down what you'll use, what you won't and how much storage you need. When I was subscribed to the Individual plan, I could have skated by with the 50GB of iCloud storage, but paying an additional $13 per month for Apple News+ was a pain. Before upgrading to Premier, I was paying about $38 per month when accounting for News+ and 200GB of iCloud Storage. At that rate, switching over to upgrade to 2TB of storage was well worth it, and it even included Apple Fitness+.
In case you weren't aware, every Apple subscription within Apple One is already shareable with a Family Sharing group — with the exception of Apple Music, which requires the Family plan for multi-person access. But if your family only cares about playing the best Apple Arcade games, for example, you could pay $7/month for that and make it available to your Family Sharing group. Apple One makes the most sense when you'll use everything.
What if I need more iCloud storage?
You can always tack on extra iCloud storage by subscribing to iCloud+, letting you max out at 14TB of storage if you get the 12TB iCloud+ plan for $60 per month alongside Apple One Premier. While you share the pool of storage, your files are not visible to other family plan members unless you so choose.
If you're already subscribed to iCloud+ with a plan that has less storage than your chosen Apple One plan, the former will be canceled, keeping any stored data intact, and you'll get a pro-rated refund. Meanwhile, if your active iCloud+ plan has more storage than your Apple One tier offers, you can keep your current plan alongside the storage Apple One provides. In case you don't need all that space, you can cancel iCloud+.
When you jump to Apple One, if you're subscribed to individual Apple services, don't worry about getting charged twice. You'll stop being billed for any individual services included in whichever Apple One plan you choose.

title_en: 10 useful iPad apps that could make your daily life easier
title_fa: 10 useful iPad apps that could make your daily life easier
excerpt_en: Your iPad can do a lot with the right apps. Go beyond Apple's defaults and try these useful offerings that all have great free tiers.
excerpt_fa: Your iPad can do a lot with the right apps. Go beyond Apple's defaults and try these useful offerings that all have great free tiers.
content_en:
10 useful iPad apps that could make your daily life easier
Put your iPad to good use with apps for journaling, discovering art and much more.
Your iPad should make every day easier. Whether you want to build new habits or improve your routines, we've rounded up apps that put the best iPads to work in your daily life.
We found these by digging a bit deeper. These aren't first-party Apple apps or subscription-only Adobe staples. It's free to get started with each, though most charge for extra features, which we've noted where applicable.
Our favorite apps are elegant and well-designed, taking advantage of the entire iPad display. They also keep AI to a bare minimum. There may be machine learning to help with search and transcriptions, but you won't find fake images or bogus text generators here.
1. Sofa: downtime organizer
If you're a voracious consumer of media, you need Sofa to help keep track of it all. Start with books, TV shows and movies, then add whatever other categories you'd like. Sofa has a clean interface that grabs title images and info to give you an overview of everything you watch (or read).
Sofa's tracking feature is especially useful for remembering which episodes you've seen. Mark them off as you watch them and add notes if you like, or rely on the included summaries. Sofa tracks two different series at once for free, while paid subscribers can track unlimited titles.
Sofa's free tier offers all its best features without advertisements or pop-ups begging for more. If you want to fine-tune your media tracking with custom ratings that you create and smart lists that populate based on your filters, Sofa offers a subscription for $5.99 per month, $49.99 per year or $249.99 for a lifetime membership. Unless you're a professional TV critic, you'll likely be fine with the free features.
2. Bear: Markdown notes
Instead of Apple Notes or Google Keep, try Bear, an app for capturing thoughts. Bear has become a productivity favorite by keeping its interface deceptively simple; it's a large notepad app without a glut of buttons and menus. While it's powerful, you don't have to use advanced features you don't need.
Bear is built around smooth Markdown styling and supports tags to organize your thoughts. For example, if you find yourself often complaining about your job, tag that post with #job. You can add links, tags or even to-do tasks that are easily searchable. If that sounds complicated, ignore what you don't need and you're left with an elegant, attractive note-taking and journaling app.

title_en: Why you shouldn't remove the screen protector film on your Nintendo Switch 2
title_fa: Why you shouldn't remove the screen protector film on your Nintendo Switch 2
excerpt_en: The Switch 2 comes with a protective film on its screen, and you may be tempted to peel it off. Here's why you shouldn't.
excerpt_fa: The Switch 2 comes with a protective film on its screen, and you may be tempted to peel it off. Here's why you shouldn't.
content_en:
Why you shouldn't remove the screen protector film on your Nintendo Switch 2
Don't do it!
We're now a little over one year into the launch of the Nintendo Switch 2, which first hit the market back in the middle of 2025. It was priced in the same ballpark as its competitors, the PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S, at $450 for the base console and $500 for a Mario Kart World bundle. Since then, it has increased to a standard $500, even for a base edition.
No one likes high prices, but if you paid either of those dollar amounts for the Switch 2, you've become keenly aware of your investment in this little machine. Keeping that investment safe is paramount, and one way to prevent damage is to avoid something that Nintendo has continuously warned us about even before launch: removing the pre-installed screen protector.
It may not seem like much, but it is a critical piece of the system's configuration. Removing it may seem tempting, but it's actually going to do quite a bit to protect your $500 investment.
The purpose of the pre-installed Nintendo Switch 2 screen protector
When we buy a new piece of hardware or device, the satisfaction of peeling a film off is remarkably enjoyable. If you have a brand-new Switch 2, however, it's recommended that you absolutely not do that. It may seem like it's there for shipping needs, but its true purpose is rather important to the overall health and longevity of the system.
Calling it a "screen protector" isn't even entirely accurate, as it's described by Nintendo as an anti-scattering adhesive film. The main purpose of the film is to protect the console from glass shards that may shatter if the screen is broken. Needless to say, it plays a critical role in the system's lifespan.
Thankfully, actually removing it is quite difficult. Removing the film requires some intense force, which is probably the first and only clue one needs to determine that it shouldn't be taken off. If you do, somehow, manage to get it off, the system will be in severe danger. It is a foundational part of the console's hardware.
Steps you can take to further protect your Nintendo Switch 2
Now that you know why you shouldn't ever remove the adhesive film from the console, you may be curious to know if the Switch 2 needs any extra protection. While you will likely get by just fine with Nintendo's pre-installed protection, there are some extra steps you can take to give your Switch 2 a bit of extra life in the years ahead.
Nintendo sells an affordable screen protector that is manufactured by HORI, and there are so many third-party aftermarket versions available for purchase that it would be almost impossible for you to not be able to find one you like. Unlike the one applied by Nintendo, an actual screen protector will do exactly that, safeguarding the console from scratches and cosmetic damage.
Tempered glass protectors will cost slightly more, depending on the brand, but this is a part of the console's accessory lineup that is actually reasonably priced when compared to other items. If you're at all worried about the screen on your Switch 2, your best course of action is to do as instructed by Nintendo and leave the film on, then grab yourself a decently priced tempered glass screen protector.

title_en: Why you should never put your PlayStation 5 on a carpeted floor
title_fa: Why you should never put your PlayStation 5 on a carpeted floor
excerpt_en: The PlayStation 5 needs to stay cool when playing games, and a carpet is a literal hotbed. Here's the best ways to store a PS5 while keeping it cool.
excerpt_fa: The PlayStation 5 needs to stay cool when playing games, and a carpet is a literal hotbed. Here's the best ways to store a PS5 while keeping it cool.
content_en:
Why you should never put your PlayStation 5 on a carpeted floor
Your PS5 needs a better home than a carpet, and you should keep the vents clear, wherever it ends up.
Sony is a bit ambiguous about the PlayStation 5 and carpeted flooring. Whether you read the downloadable PDF guide or the PlayStation Blog, it references avoiding long-fiber carpet only. However, there are three different PS5s in play, which include the Slim, the PS5 Pro and the original model. The original has no vents on its vertical base, while the Slim and the Pro have small vents on the vertical base and come with little rail stands for horizontal placement. With that knowledge, it's reasonable to assume a Slim and Pro can sit horizontally on carpet, and a first-gen PS5 with its base is fine vertically. But with Sony's basic, innocuous statement to go on, there are no distinguishing suggestions for each.
To be clear, you shouldn't place any PS5s on a short-pile or long-pile carpet, because the issue is what's hiding there. Even if you clean it regularly, carpet is a super magnet for every spore, dead skin flake, dust mote, virus and bacteria you can imagine. It's a cornucopia of tiny terror frenzies that, if viewed under a microscope, would have you ripping your carpet out the same day. And you're placing your vent ports within 1 or 2 inches of it.
Besides, putting any console on the floor is practically begging for it to get stepped on or kicked. Long-pile carpets hide things like Lego bricks, gleefully awaiting the approach of bare feet. Step on one of those and you're falling on your PS5 before you know what bit the bottom of your foot. Horizontal is better on a short-pile carpet, but again, those vents are awfully close to an around-the-clock collection of microscopic horrors. If your PS5, regardless of model, has been on carpeted flooring for a while, it's time to make a change and do a PS5 console cleaning to boot.
Give your PS5 a solid surface and some breathing room
A small table or an open TV stand is a much better accommodation for a PS5, so long as the console has plenty of room around it. Sony recommends a minimum of 4 inches around each side of the PS5. Jamming it into a cubby hole like a book won't cut it. If that's your only option, you're better off finding a small stand rather than putting it back on the carpet. The vents need to breathe, and the optimal environment is a clean and open one.
The location and placement of a PS5 matters greatly to avoid overheating, so don't worry about whether or not the system is hidden. A Slim model is a little easier to blend in with the surrounding aesthetic, but the Pro and original models are pretty large and tall. If you have to, make the space. That is, if you want your console to last as long as possible. Over time, things change, objects get tossed on the table or someone sets something down and forgets about it. Simple mindfulness will take care of that in short order. Just keep the area clean and maintained. Now and then, give your vents a quick vacuum. Use a low-power handheld and make sure the PS5 is off and unplugged before you start.
Do PS5s overheat easily?
Not really. Like any PC that uses fans for cooling, the PS5's fan can get pretty loud at times, depending on what you're playing. That's perfectly normal for the system and isn't a reason to cut the power to the entire house and stuff the console in a freezer. It can overheat if it hasn't been maintained or the placement is terrible. Playing high-performance games for hours on a poorly maintained console in a tight bookshelf will effectively damage its internal components over time. In fact, third-party repair shops like Barrie Screen Repair note that first-gen consoles have had issues with liquid metal thermal paste displacement while in the vertical position for prolonged periods.
Crashing in the middle of a game is an obvious warning sign. Overly loud fans that never drop to a lower speed or "Your PS5 is hot" messages popping up on screen make things pretty clear as well. Fortunately, the system does have fail safes. It will shut down on its own if things get a little too warm, not only to protect internals but to prolong the PS5s lifespan. If these things are happening and your system is sitting on the carpet, take it as a sign. However, once it's off the carpet, it probably needs a routine cleaning and plenty of space to stretch its legs in the future.
If you keep the setup simple and maintain the system regularly, you should be free and clear, barring an entirely separate issue that has nothing to do with carpets or cleaning.
